items.title: TACT Share Psychological Safety & Supportive Approaches at Conference
items.snippet: TACT have shared their psychological safety & supportive approaches for their staff at the National Children and Young People’s Conference 2026. The post TACT Share Psychological Safety & Supportive Approaches at Conference appeared first on TACT.
items.content:
TACT Share Psychological Safety & Supportive Approaches at Conference

On 12th November 2026, TACT’s Director of People, Daniella Jackson and Director of Children’s Services, Ramona Catarig, attended the National Children and Young People’s Conference to share how TACT is creating a psychologically safe and supportive environment for our colleagues.

Daniella and Ramona also got to meet Sam Gardner, a care-experienced speaker, former primary school teacher and creator of Lessons From The Care System – as well other amazing speakers. It was a day full of important conversations and learning.

At TACT, we believe that when our colleagues feel valued, empowered and heard, they can do their best work, which help us to create the best outcomes and positive difference to the young people and children we support. This is why we promote a wellbeing culture with lots of benefits including flexible working, wellbeing and menopause support, private health support, compressed hours, learning and development opportunities, neurodiversity communities, and more.

Thank you to the organisers for creating such a great opportunity to share ideas and learn from others across the sector.

Find out more about what it’s like to work at TACT.

items.title: TACT Young People Get Active & Creative in London & The South!
items.snippet: Our London & The South team organised a diverse programme of activities for our young people over the summer and October half term! The post TACT Young People Get Active & Creative in London & The South! appeared first on TACT.
items.content:
TACT Young People Get Active & Creative in London & The South!

Our TACT London & The South Team provided a diverse range of outdoor and creative activities for our young people over the summer and October half term – which included an awards ceremony!

The Summer Holidays

In the summer, a trip to Chessington World of Adventures was organised. It was wonderful to see so many young people attend and to celebrate everyone’s achievements together. We enjoyed a range of attractions, saw giraffes, rhinos and other animals, and the thrill seekers of the group went on rides including Mandrill Mayhem. The day also included an awards ceremony for our young people – and this was a particularly special part of the day; it provided an opportunity to recognise and celebrate the many achievements of our children and young people. The fantastic turnout made the day even more memorable, and it was wonderful to spend quality time before the summer holidays came to an end.

We also enjoyed a visit to Willows Bird of Prey Centre in Knockholt, where we learnt about a range of birds and wildlife. We watched flying demonstrations, met several birds up close and explored the wildlife trail!

A number of creative activities were also available over the summer, including pottery painting at The Paxton Centre in Crystal Palace. The session provided a relaxing space to be creative while designing and painting cups, bowls and other pottery pieces.

Cooking sessions were another highlight, with a young person learning how to make their own sushi. From preparing ingredients to rolling the sushi and choosing fillings, we enjoyed creating and tasting their finished dishes.

We also organised a YMCA residential, providing our young people with the opportunity to spend time with friends, build new relationships and take part in a wide range of activities. The residential included archery, water sports, obstacle courses, treasure hunts, climbing activities, pillow jumping and water-slide sessions. During quieter moments, there were opportunities to play football, spend time on the swings, do some colouring, play games and relax together. Evenings included movie nights and treats, providing a chance to unwind after the active days. The residential was a wonderful way to round off the summer and create positive memories before returning to school and college.

October Half Term

We started the half term week with a trip to SEA LIFE London Aquarium on the Tuesday. We all met on the steps of the aquarium on the South Bank, overlooking Big Ben and the Houses of Parliament. We could watch the boats travelling up and down the Thames as we waited. It was nice to be in central London for the day!

Once everyone had arrived, we all entered the aquarium together and then explored at our own pace. There was so much for the children to see: sharks, turtles, stingrays, seahorses and even penguins!

There were many interactive parts to the experience as we went around, including projections of polar bears and a tunnel under the aquarium tanks. There were different zones designed to simulate the animals’ various habitats – for example, a rainforest zone where you could see piranhas and a dwarf crocodile!

Continuing the excitement, our next adventure took place on the Tuesday evening, although this trip took a spookier turn!

We embarked on the woodland Halloween trail at Moors Valley Country Park as the sun went down. The trees were illuminated with different lights, and there were many eerie displays to see in the woodland clearings, including a wandering ghost bride!

The following day, keeping up the adventure, we headed to Go Ape in Kent. Those who attended were brave and were really encouraging towards each other, completing many obstacles high up in the trees and, of course, the favourite part: the zip lines over the fields.

We were lucky with the weather, and the woods looked magical. We spent a few hours up there and completed the whole course. At the end, everyone received a certificate, and we all had a picnic together.

On Thursday, we met at Spy Kids in East London, where our young people worked together to complete an assigned mission. Teamwork was paramount, and everyone did amazingly – even getting past lasers and other obstacles! The group was split into two teams, by age, to complete different missions. Afterwards everyone sat down to enjoy a meal together.

Also on the Thursday, we took some young people to visit Fishers Farm, where they could enjoy the soft play, jumping cushion, tea cups, pony rides and meeting all the animals. With such a variety of different attractions to try, there was something for everyone. One highlight was roasting marshmallows over a fire; a very cosy winter activity. Everyone got on so well and friendships developed throughout the day. We even got to try out the haunted house!

It was a really action packed half term, and while all the activities were quite different, there were the same themes of trying new things whilst making new friends.

The lovely feedback we have received from our young people has confirmed that there really was something for everyone across the summer and half term; not everyone enjoys the active outdoors or arts and crafts, so it’s important that our activities suit different age groups and interests.

A big thank you to the team for their hard work in putting together a diverse programme of events!

The post TACT Young People Get Active & Creative in London & The South! appeared first on TACT.

items.title: Celebrating Children’s Achievements In The South West
items.snippet: TACT South West celebrated its young people and foster carers at its annual Children and Young People’s Celebration Awards! The post Celebrating Children’s Achievements In The South West appeared first on TACT.
items.content:
Celebrating Children’s Achievements In The South West

TACT South West hosted their annual Children and Young People’s Celebration Awards in October, providing a chance for foster carers to express their pride in what their children and young people have achieved!

Taking place at Weston-Super-Mare Pier, the event started with one young person reading out each nomination – with every award winner received a certificate and goody bag filled with treats. Many of the nominations mentioned young people’s ‘growth in confidence’, ‘positive steps taken’, and the ‘wonderful qualities they bring into the world’. Here are just a few examples of what our foster carers wrote about our young people:

“Well done for settling in so well to your new school and home, we love how curious you are.”

“We are so proud of your determination and the huge progress you’ve made over the last year, we want you to know that your achievements deserve to be recognised.”

“You deserve to be recognised as you are inspiring, you’ve become a published author as part of the Mission Chaos Young Writers challenge and we couldn’t be prouder.”

“Congratulations on your progress you’ve made with learning English, we’re so proud of everything you’ve achieved including getting into college and hoping to soon start an apprenticeship.”

There were also a number of awards given to foster carers from children. Many expressed gratitude and how happy they were to be living with them, as well as how much their carers made them laugh and smile. It was heart-warming to see a room full of love and appreciation despite the challenges that many of the children and young people have faced in the past.

TACT foster carers, Wendy and Amanda, shared their thoughts on why events such as this are important. Wendy said: “It’s lovely to be able to celebrate both the children and carers’ achievements. To me it’s the highlight of the year. We get to meet carers we may not have seen all year and we have such different backgrounds and lifestyles that it’s nice to just catch up.”

Amanda expressed how it’s a chance to celebrate “the simplest things, like just getting up every day and going to school. It could be something bigger, but sometimes even those little things need celebrating. Just to see them getting an achievement – it makes me so proud.”

The awards were followed by a buffet lunch which allowed children to catch up with friends as well as letting foster carers spend time with their support networks. Everyone then headed into the arcade for some fun and games before heading home.

It’s extremely important to everyone involved that events like these take place; it provides foster carers and young people with a chance to acknowledge and celebrate even the smallest of achievements. Sometimes it is the small achievements and wins that make the most difference.

A big thank you to our young people, foster carers and staff for their time and commitment. The day was a huge success and many were expressing how much they were already looking forward to doing it again next year!

The post Celebrating Children’s Achievements In The South West appeared first on TACT.

One of the most common myths about fostering is that you can't become a foster parent if you already have young children of your own.

In reality, many fostering families have children living at home. Every household is unique, and the most important thing is being able to meet the needs of all the children in your home and create a safe, supportive environment where everyone can thrive.

Meet Joy! 👋

For Joy Hunt, Head of Fostering in our West Region, it's the people who make fostering so special. 💚

Having started her career in residential childcare before moving into fostering, Joy has spent her working life helping children feel safe, valued and supported.

Now, 18 months into her role as Head of Fostering, she says it's a privilege to work alongside such an incredible community of foster parents and colleagues.

What inspires her most? The patience, resilience and dedication of our foster parents, who go above and beyond every day to give children the love, stability and opportunities they deserve.

Joy is particularly proud of the West Region's experienced foster parents who care for younger children, helping them feel safe and secure as they prepare for the next chapter in their lives.

And when she's not championing our fostering families? You'll probably find Joy at the stables with her daughter, enjoying time with her horses, or escaping to the Welsh countryside for some fresh air and a little peace and quiet! 🐴

For Joy, fostering is all about relationships, and making sure no foster parent feels they're on that journey alone.

We're lucky to have Joy leading our West Region fostering community! 💚

items.title: ‘Happy Birthday’ to TACT’s Health Service!
items.snippet: As TACT's Health Service celebrates its first birthday under its Framework Contract arrangement, Health Commissioning Manager, Mechelle, reflects on its true goal. The post ‘Happy Birthday’ to TACT’s Health Service! appeared first on TACT.
items.content:
‘Happy Birthday’ to TACT’s Health Service!

As TACT’s dedicated and specialist Health Service celebrates its first birthday, Mechelle Holley, TACT’s Health Commissioning & Performance Manager, reflects on this important milestone.

27th October 2026 marked a milestone for me on my journey with TACT: our Health Service under its new Framework Contract arrangement celebrated its first birthday. I know it’s strange to recognise it as a birthday, and not an anniversary, but it really does feel like something I’ve helped to shape and nurture into what we have today, and ‘birthday’ feels like the right words to use.

Looking back, it’s fair to say that TACT started this journey with a huge amount of ambition, passion and vision for a service which could be as unique and individual as the children and young people it supports. Something which could bend and flex to changing needs and demands rather than being built around a single approach or model of therapeutic intervention.

When people ask me to describe the framework, I often compare it to Heinz 57 varieties. With every intervention offering something slightly different, there is a huge choice and expertise that means we are far more likely to find something that feels right for the individual child, young person, carer or professional seeking support.

The world of commissioning can sit quite awkwardly within children’s social care. The language used can feel quite transactional and make people feel we forget the humanity or the person at the centre of the work, or that there’s an overly strong focus on money. A key part of my role over the last 12 months has been to help navigate between these two worlds, translating the awkward, technical contract and financial language into real, tangible benefits which children, young people, foster carers and the professionals around them can feel and see.

“The real measure of our success is whether children and young people, foster carers and the professionals who work tirelessly to support them can access the support they need, when they need it.”

Mechelle Holley, TACT’s Health Commissioning & Performance Manager

I’m very aware that the success of the framework is only as good as the difference that it can make. Whilst contracts, procurement activity, tender awards and building a network of partners we trust were important, they were never the goal. The real measure of our success is whether children and young people, foster carers and the professionals who work tirelessly to support them can access the support they need, when they need it.

Psychological assessments were a new addition to TACT’s established therapeutic offer. By taking a holistic, multi-agency approach to understanding a child’s experiences and journey, we can develop a richer understanding of their needs and help ensure that pathways for their future are reflective and responsive to their individuality. For young people who have struggled to have their needs met, this type of understanding can be transformative.

A TACT Supervising Social Worker in our West Midlands team reflected on one young person’s experience; despite years of advocacy from their foster carers, they had ‘fallen through the gaps’ of NHS services. The introduction of the framework contract enabled access to a full psychological and cognitive assessment, which provided greater clarity of their needs and ensured they had access to the support needed both now, and in the future.

One additional aspect I’m particularly proud of with the introduction of assessment provision is TACT’s decision to provide a dedicated budget for the Health Service, allowing us to contribute towards the cost of assessments. For me, TACT’s values are incredibly important – and being able to live these through the work we do matters greatly. We truly demonstrate the shared commitment TACT has with local authorities to improve the lives of the children and young people we are entrusted to care for, rather than allowing funding arrangements and organisational boundaries to become a barrier to support – something I have seen often in previous commissioning roles.

However, assessments are only one part of the offer. Over the last year, the framework has allowed TACT’s area teams to develop a range of alternative therapeutic approaches which reflect the individuality of their geographical needs. These have ranged from introducing monthly group-themed learning and reflection spaces for foster carers and staff, to offering dedicated therapeutic consultation sessions for the team around a child to discuss specific, individual challenges. These opportunities ensure that TACT continues to hold space for reflection and to ensure we continue to provide trauma-informed and personalised care.

The last 12 months have given lots of opportunity for learning, both for me personally and TACT as an organisation. Change is never an easy process to manage, particularly when it introduces new ways of working and in a world where there is much change going on externally across the health and social care sectors. For me, it feels like the Health Service Framework Contract is becoming increasingly embedded across TACT, with growing levels of awareness, confidence and increased access across area teams.

Recently, I’ve been working hard behind the scenes to conclude a tender review and refresh activity and I’m excited that we’ve added a number of new partners, which strengthens our offer and ability to provide timely support. Whilst I am incredibly proud of what we have achieved, I believe this isn’t the end of the journey and there’s so much more we can do. I’m looking forward to continuing to develop the offer, partnering with new providers and ensuring we can apply the same commissioning and procurement lenses to all therapeutic partners, including those where the professional relationship pre-dates the introduction of the Framework Contract.

If this first year has taught me anything, it’s that when we combine aspiration, vision and innovation we can create meaningful and lasting changes which create new and exciting opportunities to support children and young people to thrive. For me, this first birthday feels like just the beginning.

Mechelle Holley, TACT’s Health Commissioning & Performance Manager

items.title: Meet Chelsea Noble: Supervising Social Worker
items.snippet: Chelsea has worked in fostering for nearly ten years, but her route into social work was not a straight line. The post Meet Chelsea Noble: Supervising Social Worker appeared first on Swiis Foster Care.
items.content:
Chelsea has worked in fostering for nearly ten years, but her route into social work was not a straight line. She started out in finance, then began volunteering with a charity supporting a young person with learning disabilities. She enjoyed it so much that she moved into fostering, joining an agency admin team in 2017 and working her way up to social work.

In April 2023, she qualified as a social worker and joined Swiis earlier this year as a Supervising Social Worker for our Midlands & South team, covering the South West.

Day to day, she supports our foster carers with training, annual reviews and ongoing approval, gives them space to talk things through, and works closely with local authorities to keep the best interests of every child at the centre of everything she does.

Outside work, Chelsea enjoys running and crafting, and she is currently working on a diamond painting. She also has two house rabbits, who she calls her “little colleagues at home.”

We sat down with Chelsea to learn more about her journey to becoming a Supervising Social Worker, what her role involves, and how she supports our foster carers and children.

Chelsea’s Fostering Story

How did you get into social work?

“I was working in finance and decided it was time for a change. I started volunteering with a charity called Time to Share, supporting a young person with learning disabilities, and I really enjoyed it. I realised I could make more of an impact and support people. I always wanted to work in health and social care when I was at school, but I did a complete U-turn and studied travel and tourism instead. So, it is quite funny that I have ended up back here, about ten years later.”

What inspired you to pursue a career in fostering?

“Growing up, I had a friend whose parents were foster carers, so children and young people would come and stay with them. I was always fascinated by it. I used to hear about it from his point of view as a birth child, how it affected him and the support he could have benefited from. I think, deep down, that is why I came into fostering, and I want to stay here. My first insight into the fostering world was a temporary admin role, and I have worked my way through different roles since.”

Is there a moment in your career that has stayed with you?

During her social work training, Chelsea completed a placement with a local authority, supporting a family through a very difficult time. She helped find a foster home for a young person she had built a strong relationship with.

“I am still in touch with my supervisor, and she tells me how well he is getting on. He went to college and he is thriving. It gave me a real insight into the other side, what life is like for young people coming into care. I bring that knowledge into my work every day.”

Can you share a foster carer success story?

“We have just had one. A young person who has lived with her foster carer for the last couple of years has thrived academically and has just gone off to university to study pharmacy. She did not quite get the grades she wanted, but she persevered. Her PEP [Personal Education Plan] meetings were always so positive, and I think that is down to her foster carer, who has been so supportive and really helped her take that step into her next chapter.”

What do you enjoy most about supporting foster carers and children in care?

“It is the little successes. When children first come into care, they can be very unsettled, and then even after a couple of months you see how much they change, physically and emotionally. Those fundamental things that many of us take for granted can really ground them. Helping foster carers provide that is what I find most rewarding.”

Chelsea’s Fostering Insight

What would you like people to know about fostering?

“Fostering is open to so many people. A lot of people think it is only for those who already have children, or for older people, but younger foster carers can be fantastic too. I supported a young couple at my last agency who were fantastic, and they could really relate to the young person in their care. Same-sex couples, the LGBTQ+ community, single people: anyone can foster. One of the best foster carers I have worked with was a single mum with two children of her own and three young people in her care. She was a super mum, with a great support network around her.”

Why is support so important?

“It sounds like a cliché, but it takes a village. That is what a lot of our foster carers love about Swiis: you are part of a team. Our Stability and Support team is amazing, so if I am out on visits, foster carers always have someone else to talk to. It is also about the people around you who can offer practical and emotional support, because fostering can be challenging as well as rewarding.”

How does your work benefit children and young people?

“By giving foster carers the skills, knowledge and emotional support they need to care for children and young people who have experienced trauma and big changes in their lives. Our events also bring foster families together, and children and young people realise they are not the only ones in care. They can say, ‘You have a social worker, I have a social worker,’ and talk about things they might not share with other friends.”

What advice would you give to someone considering fostering?

“Be open-minded, be honest and be willing to learn. No one has all the answers, and that includes us. Work with the team around you and enjoy the happy moments, because there are lots of them. We are always honest about the challenges, but fostering is a very rewarding career.”

If you are thinking about fostering, why not do the Can I Foster Quiz, or contact our lovely recruitment team, who will be happy to walk you through the fostering process. Alternatively, have a read of our Fostering Info Pack for information on fostering and fostering with Swiis.

items.title: TACT Carers Win Foster Carer Award at National Children and Young People Awards!
items.snippet: Congratulations to two TACT fostering households, who have won National Children and Young People Awards at the 2026 ceremony! The post TACT Carers Win Foster Carer Award at National Children and Young People Awards! appeared first on TACT.
items.content:
TACT Carers Win Foster Carer Award at National Children and Young People Awards!

A huge congratulations to Jon and Ellen Evans for winning the Foster Carer Award, and to Sandra Cornwall for receiving the highly commended award at the National Children and Young People Awards!

Get to know our winners:

The Foster Carer Award Winner: Ellen and Jon Evans

When we found out we had been nominated for the National Children and Young People awards, initially it was shock as although we have been on this medically complex and emotional journey, to us this is our family life. However, we both felt a sense of pride for having the acknowledgment of what we do.

On our first date, we actually discussed wanting to become foster carers one day in the future! Life continued, we had a daughter, got married and worked in our chosen fields. However, the seed we had planted on that first date many years ago grew, and we decided it was the right time to look into fostering.

For myself, I had worked with a birth family where the child was removed due to significant neglect and physical harm. I went to visit this child in a foster home and the difference in him was outstanding. In the short period of time, he looked so healthy and has started to catch up on some of his delayed milestones, but most of all, to see the emotional attachment he was able to form and the love and care he was given was inspirational, and at this point I knew in my heart, I could do this.

For us, the most rewarding part of our journey has been watching J develop despite everything he has been through. He has the most beautiful soul, his smile lights up the room and recently seeing his emotional development makes us so proud.

J has had periods of being gravely unwell, during covid he had a significant bleed on his brain post operatively. During this time, he was placed on a ventilator, and we were told that they were unsure if he had the ability to breath on his own due to the brain damage. The moment we will never forget is when that ventilator was removed, he overcame the odds and was able to breath. We will never forget that feeling of overwhelming emotion that he has survived, I can not express in words how that moment felt.

Having only cared for one child over the last seven years, we can only express how he has changed us.

J is a little boy who has undergone so much, prior to the significant brain injury he had already undergone five brain surgeries and open heart surgery. Despite his life changing injuries  such as going blind, needing a permanent feeding tube, being unable to move unaided, we have never know a child who is so happy, his smile is infectious and recently he has really started to belly laugh, he has taught us the purity of joy in life.

To us being a foster carer has meant opening up our hearts. This is where it starts, you must genuinely care for a child, provide stability, love and commitment. It means not doing something half heartedly, you need to be committed. Throughout our journey with J, we have experienced extreme highs and lows with regards to his health. The motivation is simple, it comes from him. Knowing his needs come first. It can be emotionally hard facing things, for example, recently we have been part of the advanced care plan which also looks at end of life care. Emotionally, this is something we did not want to face, however our motivation to be part of this came from him. The fear of losing him it’s great however the need to ensure he always feels safe, never alone and loved has to come before our own emotional need. The motivation comes from him and the life we share for him.

Recognition of our journey is amazing. In one respect it feels strange as this is our life daily caring for J needs physically, emotionally and medically. Living and caring for a medically complex child has become our norm so having this recognition does make us acknowledge this achievement.

To me being a foster carer has provided me with the opportunity to care for the most amazing little boy. It has provided me with many learning opportunities. I have learnt more about myself and my abilities to advocate and that I have more resilience that I thought possible.

Highly Commendable Winner: Sandra Cornwall

My journey to become a foster carer started 22 years ago when I had a supervision session with my manager, and during that supervision, she suggested to me that she thought I would be good as a foster carer, because I was always supportive of others, and at the time she had never known a single parent to get 3 kids under the age of 7 in bed by 7.30pm!

The most rewarding part of my fostering journey has been seeing the young people and young mothers leave my home with their babies and go on to thrive in the community.

Being a Foster Carer personally means to me being open to show young people that there are good people in the world who can make a difference to their life, to believe in them, encourage them to thrive and be happy. Having a supportive supervising social worker and family has been my motivation to keep going through the challenges.

To me, being a Foster Carer has been the most amazing journey I have been on throughout my life, and I can’t see this journey finishing any time soon. I have too much love to give.

TACT’s Education Service to Equip Foster Carers with Advocacy Skills
items.snippet: TACT is to provide their foster carers with specific guidance on advocating for children during education meetings. The post TACT’s Education Service to Equip Foster Carers with Advocacy Skills appeared first on TACT.
items.content:
TACT’s Education Service to Equip Foster Carers with Advocacy Skills

TACT is to provide their foster carers with guidance on helping them to advocate for children within an educational context, especially where they have concerns around unmet additional needs.

The need for this guidance was highlighted by TACT’s dedicated Education Service, when the team noticed patterns in many of the geographical areas they operate in: that carers were in need of specific support to be able to articulate their concerns in education meetings.

TACT have commissioned Pooky Knightsmith, who has a PhD in Psychological Medicine from the Institute of Psychiatry, to run a training session for the charity. She said: “When you live with a child, you know things nobody else in the [education] meeting knows. The hard part is working out which of those things matter, finding the words for them, and keeping the conversation going when professionals describe a child you don’t recognise.

“This session looks at what’s going on for children whose needs are shaped by both their neurology and their early experiences, then at the practical side of meetings: who’s in the room and what you’re entitled to say, what to gather beforehand, what to ask for, and where to go next if the answer is no.”

After the session, foster carers should be able to:

  • Gather evidence that carries weight in meetings
  • Describe what happens at home so it’s taken seriously
  • Get the jargon explained in plain English
  • Hold a different view without falling out with anyone
  • Ask for the adjustments most likely to help
  • Follow up in a way that keeps things moving

Foster carers are provided with a small set of tools to keep and reuse: a meeting planning sheet, a ‘fill in the blanks’ follow up template, and a bank of reasonable adjustments to ask about.

A big thank you to our Education Service for adding an additional level to the amazing support they already provide to our foster carers.

items.title: Celebrating Bee’s 20 Years of Fostering with Swiis
items.snippet: Bee has supported babies, teenagers, sibling groups, parent and child arrangements, sanctuary seeking young people and children in long term foster care. The post Celebrating Bee’s 20 Years of Fostering with Swiis appeared first on Swiis Foster Care.
items.content:
For 20 years, Bee has been changing the lives of children and young people through fostering. What began as a chance encounter with Swiis at a recruitment event in Leeds has grown into a remarkable journey during which she has cared for more than 50 children and young people.

Bee has supported babies, teenagers, sibling groups, parent and child arrangements, sanctuary seeking young people and children in long term foster care. Along the way, she has built lasting relationships that continue long after young people leave her home.

At the heart of Bee’s fostering journey has always been family. When she began fostering, her son Ashley was 20 years old and living at home. Together, alongside Bee’s wider family network of nieces, siblings and extended relatives, they created a home where children and young people felt welcomed, supported and valued.

“It is just part of all our lives, not just mine. The whole family is involved. We are all part of a family network.”

Today, some of the children Bee cared for are now adults with families of their own, while many former young people continue to stay in touch, regularly visiting, calling for advice and celebrating milestones together. For Bee, fostering has never simply been about providing a home. It has been about creating lifelong connections.

Looking Back: What Inspired You to Become a Foster Carer?

Bee spent many years working in hospitality and caring for friends’ children before she became a foster carer.

“I was looking after friends’ children long before I became a foster carer. I was on a rare day off from the public house I was running and went to Leeds with my niece. Swiis was in the library doing a recruitment drive and my niece said, ‘You enjoy looking after children, so you should apply?’ I gave my details, started the process and here I am 20 years later.”

“I have a big heart and would always find room for other children. With my son being an only child, it was company for him as well.”

Why did you decide to foster Teenagers?

While Bee has cared for children of all ages throughout her fostering career, teenagers have always held a special place in her heart. Her passion stems from seeing young people grow, challenge themselves and gradually develop confidence and independence.

“I have always said I only want teenagers. I love them. I know some people want babies, but I wanted teenagers. The stroppier the better. They are funny. They challenge you all the time, but that is how they learn.”

Bee believes building trust is key, particularly for young people who have experienced instability.

“They are looking to see how you react and whether you are still going to be there for them because they are not used to it.”

Creating an Extended Family

One of the most rewarding parts of fostering for Bee has been maintaining relationships with young people long after they have left her care.

Her first care arrangement remains part of her life today.

“I started with my first young man, Kevin. He is now 32 and still part of my life, and he has a 10-year-old child of his own. Some of my foster children are grown up now and I still see them. I just love that it is an extension to my family.”

For Bee, fostering is about belonging.

“When my teenagers grow up, have children of their own and are still part of each other’s lives, that is really special. They are part of my family and I am part of theirs.”

Moments That Have Stayed with Bee

Over 20 years, Bee has experienced many memorable and challenging moments.

Bee recalls being present for milestone moments in the lives of young people she supported through parent and childcare arrangements.

“Being present for the births of babies to two mothers I supported was very special. They said, ‘We want Bee there,’ and being able to cut a baby’s cord was really special.”

The Importance of Support

Throughout her fostering journey, Bee says the support she has received from Swiis has played a significant role in her success.

In particular, she values the consistency provided by her supervising social worker.

“What is great for me and my young people is the relationship they have with Vanessa. They can talk to her, they have a laugh, and when we need support with anything, she is there for us. I have had Vanessa for eight or nine years and that continuity helps build confidence, relationships and trust. Having the same supervising social worker gives them much needed consistency.”

What Is Bee Most Proud Of?

After fostering more than 50 children and young people, Bee’s proudest achievement is not the number of arrangements she has supported. Instead, it is the relationships that have lasted.

“Seeing them grow up, have children of their own and still want you in their lives, that is special. Making it to 20 years and still feeling the same passion I felt when I started is also something I am proud of.”

Bee’s Advice for Anyone Considering Fostering

Bee is honest that fostering can be challenging, but she believes it is one of the most rewarding things someone can do. She also encourages prospective foster carers to listen and learn from experienced foster carers.

“You need to be a good communicator, be transparent and listen. Be able to listen to the children. Come and meet other foster carers because we all have our own stories to tell.”

“It is hard. It is not an easy job. The children will push your buttons, and you have to manage that by using your support network, training and team.”

Most importantly, Bee believes fostering is about partnership.

“It is about teamwork. You and that young person are the team, and then you have got the bigger team around you.”

Thank You, Bee

As Bee celebrates 20 years with Swiis, we would like to thank her for her commitment, compassion and unwavering dedication to children and young people.

Having cared for more than 50 children and young people across a wide range of care arrangements, while building relationships that have continued into adulthood, Bee’s story demonstrates the lasting difference a foster carer can make.

If Bee’s story has inspired you to learn more about fostering, book your place on one of our Introduction to Fostering webinars. You will have the opportunity to hear directly from our team, learn more about the fostering journey and ask any questions you may have in a supportive and informal setting.

items.title: My Visit to 10 Downing Street
items.snippet: TACT CEO, Andy Elvin, was invited to attend Downing Street, for the launch of the Department for Education's fostering recruitment campaign. The post My Visit to 10 Downing Street appeared first on TACT.
items.content:
My Visit to 10 Downing Street

TACT CEO, Andy Elvin, was invited to attend 10 Downing Street for the launch of a national fostering recruitment campaign.

On Tuesday 13th October 2026, I was privileged to be invited to 10 Downing Street for the launch of the Department for Education (DfE) fostering recruitment campaign in England. It was a great event with some fantastic and inspirational speakers. The event was opened and hosted by Marie France Van Heel , the Prime Minister’s wife. It was her first time hosting an event since moving into Downing Street and she spoke excellently and passionately about the importance of foster care. She shared that she had thought of fostering, but her husband’s job made that challenging. It was pointed out to her that her new home had plenty of spare rooms!

The main speaker was Amy Burns, host of ‘Messy Fostering’; she spoke movingly and frankly about her experience of fostering and left the room in no doubt about the importance of fostering and the urgent need to ensure that all children who need fostering can be provided with safe, stable & loving foster homes.

This is only the second dedicated fostering event at 10 Downing Street and it was great to see that fostering is now front and centre of the government’s plans for the care system.

It was brilliant to see so many people who were determined to increase the availability of foster care and transform outcomes for our children and young people. I caught up with Brad Keller and took his photo for him outside number 10. Brad is keen to do all he can to support fostering as he credits his foster family for inspiring him and encouraging him to follow his passion for music.

“With the rise of Regional Care Co-Ops, the national foster carer recruitment campaign, the new National Minimum Standards and the various innovation projects that we are involved with, this is a good time for fostering. It is vital that we take full advantage of this so we can improve outcomes for our children,  young people & care-experienced community.”

Andy Elvin, TACT CEO

Huge credit goes to Children’s Minister Josh MacAlister for organising the event and putting fostering at the centre of things so early in Andy Burnham’s premiership.

I also met a couple of the Traitors cast, Judy and Roxy, who were keen to promote fostering and were both hilarious and excellent company.

It was also good to see so many partners and friends of ours including Niketa Sanderson-Gillard, who has drafted the new National Minimum Standards, Allan Madeley from Home fostering, Sarah Thomas – CEO of The Fostering Network, Katie and Sara from Now Foster, and Ashley John Baptiste.

With the rise of Regional Care Co-Ops, the national foster carer recruitment campaign, the new National Minimum Standards and the various innovation projects that we are involved with, this is a good time for fostering. It is vital that we take full advantage of this so we can improve outcomes for our children,  young people & care-experienced community – and support our foster families in doing this. With the new legislation in Scotland meaning all Independent Fostering Agencies must be charities and the ‘eliminate profit’ agenda in Wales, there are positive signs for fostering across the UK.

TACT are central to all of these developments and initiatives and we will continue to advocate for fostering and all of the children, young people and care-experienced adults who it is our privilege to care for.

Their selfless dedication, courage and determination embody TACT’s promise of ‘more than just fostering’. They do not simply meet J’s needs, they help him thrive.
  • Sandra: Sandra’s loyalty, compassion and determination show selfless dedication in its truest form. She has gone far beyond providing day-to-day care, she has remained his advocate, his constant and an important source of security when he has needed it most. Sandra’s sustained commitment through the most challenging of circumstances makes her an outstanding candidate for The Foster Carer Award.
  • Lyn and Jim: Lyn and Jim embody the selflessness at the heart of fostering, steadfast commitment, compassion in action and an unwavering belief in L’s potential. They have not simply provided care; they have offered lasting belonging and built their family life around helping him flourish.
  • Angela and Charlene: Angela and Charlene’s selfless dedication has enabled K not only to cope, but to thrive.  They have offered more than stability, they have provided belonging, hope and the freedom to grow.
  • Alison and Frankie: Across their 13.5 years, they have offered far more than practical care; they have provided belonging, opportunity and enduring commitment. Their values remain constant. They preserve meaningful relationships, continue to offer time and connection. When things don’t go to plan, they reflect, avoid taking responses personally and continue to speak about children with warmth and pride. This demonstrates rare perseverance and unconditional care.

We’re so proud of each and every one of you. We’ll be cheering you all on and keeping our fingers crossed!

The National Children and Young People Awards were established to ‘celebrate excellence in the care for children, young people and families, showcase innovation and best practice in this area and pay tribute to those individuals or organisation who excel in quality care provision’. The awards recognise individuals working in care homes, local authorities, fostering and adoption services or the voluntary sectors.

items.title: TACT Welcomes ‘Next Phase’ in Ending Foster Care Profits in Wales
items.snippet: TACT has voiced its support for the Welsh Government's next steps in eliminating profit making within the fostering sector. The post TACT Welcomes ‘Next Phase’ in Ending Foster Care Profits in Wales appeared first on TACT.
items.content:
TACT Welcomes ‘Next Phase’ in Ending Foster Care Profits in Wales

The Welsh Government’s bid to remove private profit from the care of children looked after in Wales is set to move into its second phase. TACT is in support of the move – having already played an active part in their own campaign to remove profit from foster care.

Whilst the Welsh Government set out their plans to remove profit from children’s services in 2025 by amending their Regulation and Inspection of Social Care (Wales) Act 2016, its next phase will take effect by 1st April 2027.

The route of this change in legislation was, in part, due to a response from young people themselves. They told the Welsh Government that they were concerned about being cared for by privately owned organisations that were making a profit from their experience of being in care.

The Welsh Government’s first phase, already in effect from 1st April 2026, stated that new ‘for-profit’ fostering providers were not eligible to register with the Care Inspectorate Wales (CIW). Existing for-profit fostering agencies could still operate but would face the first of two further restrictive deadlines beginning on 1st April 2027: they will no longer be able to approve new foster carers.

The final deadline, at least at this point in time, will not come into effect until 1st April 2030, and will mean that children will not be able to be placed in a for-profit agency by an English local authority except in exceptional circumstances. Welsh local authorities will only be able to do so with the agreement of Welsh Ministers.

The changes being phased in by the Welsh Government are less about forcing for-profit fostering organisations to cease trading and more about making it unviable to profit from fostering. The deadlines allow affected agencies to transition to charitable or community-based providers if they wish to continue operating in the sector.

TACT Fostering made a commitment to the Welsh Government’s objectives in 2024 when they acquired the for-profit agency Foster Care Values (FCV), based in Conwy, North Wales. Andy Elvin, CEO of TACT Fostering, said: “Foster Care Values is an excellent fostering agency with whom we share many values and an ethos that puts children and young people at the heart of all that we do, but as a family-owned and run for-profit agency, their model was not aligned with the Welsh government plans. This partnership has provided stability and reassurance of a long-term future, for the children, staff and foster carers.”

A key focus for TACT Fostering has always been to help instigate change in the fostering sector at a governmental level. However, with their CEO also the chair of The Fairer Fostering Partnership, an umbrella organisation representing charitable and not-for-profit fostering providers, profit making in foster care has always been a key topic on their agenda; the charity would like to see the removal of profit from the fostering sector on a national level.

World Mental Health Day: Being a Mental Health First Aider
items.snippet: This World Mental Health Day, TACT staff member Dan shares his experience of being a trained Mental Health First Aider The post World Mental Health Day: Being a Mental Health First Aider appeared first on TACT.
items.content:
World Mental Health Day: Being a Mental Health First Aider

It’s World Mental Health Day on 10th October, so we’re shining a light on the work of Mental Health First Aiders (MHFA). Mental Health First Aid is the help offered to a person developing a mental health issue, experiencing a worsening of an existing mental health issue or in a mental health crisis. The first aid is given until appropriate professional help is received or until the crisis appear to have been resolved.

We spoke to Dan, one of several Mental Health First Aiders at TACT.

My experience as a mental health first aider

I’ve always wanted to help other people in some capacity, but always felt like I had the empathy bit in place, but not necessarily the skills to back it up. When I found out that TACT provided the opportunity for staff to train as Mental Health First Aiders, and then to join a dedicated support team, it was a no-brainer for me. Being a Mental Health First Aider means I get the opportunity to put something back into TACT, whilst also fulfilling a want to help other people that has been with me for a long time. The most rewarding part of being a MHFA so far is actually using some of the skills I’ve learned to help support those outside of TACT.

I think having Mental Health First Aiders at TACT is important because, even if we’re not called upon in a direct sense, I like to think that the knowledge that there is a support team available across many of our departments is reassuring.

During my Mental Health First Aider Training, I learnt that active listening and validation of another person’s feelings can go a long way to being helpful in a moment of distress. I have also learned not to be a ‘fixer’; MHFAers are there not to solve problems, but to listen, validate and signpost. MHFAers are provided with a dedicated app that can be used to find professional support platforms specific to area, need and whether support would be best accessed online or in person.

You don’t need to be a MHFA to help

If you aren’t a Mental Health First Aider, there are still many things that you can do to help support someone.

The most important thing is to be a good active listener – which involves providing your full attention and showing empathy. Not automatically filling any silences in the conversation is important; silence can be supportive too so allow conversations the space to breathe. Not trying to solve things is another important part; many people feel that they have to provide some form of solution in order to help, when in fact all that may be needed is for someone to listen.

You can also signpost to many national organisations that can provide support, such as:

  • Hub of Hope: a great initial resource, and one of the main tools MHFAers use to help signpost to relevant support.
  • Samaritans: for more immediate support over the phone (they are apparently working to set up an online chat facility): 116 123 for free, confidential, 24/7 emotional support for anyone in distress.
  • Childline: support for those aged under 19.
  • Shout: a free text messaging service which provides 24/7 support for anyone experiencing a mental health crisis.
  • Mind: provides helplines, resources and a network of local ‘Minds’.

Signposting a person to their GP or asking them to call NHS 111 is another option.

Mental health is generally getting a lot easier to talk about in lots of different environments such as schools and workplaces – with many offering their own internal support services. However, for someone experiencing a mental health crisis, sometimes the last thing they want to do is talk about it. Therefore, it is important that a safe, non-judgmental and confidential environment is provided to enable people to talk about their mental health if they need to.

If you’re feeling anxious or distressed, please talk to someone. They may not be a MHFA, but someone who you trust and you feel comfortable with. You may not initially feel like doing it, but you will be glad you did.

TACT provides a dedicated internal Health Service for young people, as well as wellbeing activities, perks and resources for their foster carers.

items.title: DfE to Launch Fostering Recruitment Campaign
items.snippet: The Department for Education is launching a co-ordinated fostering recruitment campaign in October 2026, due to a shortage of foster carers. The post DfE to Launch Fostering Recruitment Campaign appeared first on TACT.
items.content:
Department for Education to Launch Fostering Recruitment Campaign

The Department for Education (DfE) is launching its first fully co-ordinated fostering recruitment campaign in October 2026, aimed at encouraging more people to consider fostering.

The heart of the campaign is not only the dispelling of myths and misconceptions around who can foster, but also about reframing fostering as an extension of who people already are, rather than asking them to become a different kind of person. Therefore, the campaign will highlight more of the everyday differences that people can make to children’s lives, over and above any perceived complex expectations or specialist skillsets that may feel out of reach.

The campaign has arrived at a time of decreased numbers of approved foster carers in the UK. According to the DfE, the number of foster carers has fallen by 12% since 2019, with research showing that misconceptions is a driving factor in people ruling themselves out before even exploring fostering.

TACT are passionate about dispelling fostering myths and misconceptions; the charity ran a campaign in September of 2025 called ‘Ordinary People Making an Extraordinary Difference’, which highlighted the everyday smaller gestures of care that can make a positive impact on young people. Another key message of the campaign was that fostering should be an option for people across all walks of life, and not just those with care-aligned vocational backgrounds.

TACT are proud to be supporting the upcoming co-ordinated fostering recruitment campaign, and look forward to engaging with each step as they are revealed by the Department for Education.

Read more about fostering myth busting on our Fostering Questions and Answers page.

items.title: ‘Mr Gum’ Author Inspires Foster Children
items.snippet: Andy Stanton, author of the Mr Gum books, led an inspiring workshop for a group of TACT young people - in line with a year-long timetable of reading activities! The post ‘Mr Gum’ Author Inspires Foster Children appeared first on TACT.
items.content:
‘Mr Gum’ Author Inspires Foster Children

A famous author has inspired a group of TACT young people, in a workshop aimed at encouraging a passion for reading.

Andy Stanton, the celebrated author of the Mr Gum book series, led an online workshop organised by TACT Fostering – in line with their extensive year-long National Year of Reading campaign activities.

He took the participants through his own creative processes, including the time he wrote a story for his nephews on Christmas Eve (which they ignored as it was Christmas), only to find the story again years later ‘in a box’. That story became the first Mr Gum book.

No stranger to working with children, Andy said: “I’ve been talking to children in schools and at book festivals for twenty years now. I haven’t done any events or workshops for children in care before. Whomever I’m talking to I always strive to make my events inclusive and welcoming for all. 

“There’s a part of the workshop where I ask the children if they’ve ever woken up in the middle of the night with a crazy idea running through their head. I always love hearing the surprising answers that come out of that. Hopefully the children were engaged throughout, but these moments of interaction stand out [for me].”

Andy is also passionate about encouraging a love for reading in young people: “Reading can expand a young person’s horizons and make them aware that a whole world of opportunity is out there. Even if that opportunity is ‘just’ the opportunity to explore a different life or viewpoint for a while via escapist fiction – that’s invaluable and so many life lessons can be taught under cover of ‘only a story’!”

Tina Bull, an Education Advisory Teacher who works within TACT’s Education Service, echoed this sentiment: “Sessions like this, particularly when we can call on established writers and illustrators, are wonderfully inspiring for our young people.

“Throughout our sessions, if we can inspire just one of our young people to read more regularly or more widely, the work and planning for our year-long calendar of National Year of Reading activities will have been worth it.”

The National Year of Reading is a campaign aimed at bringing the joy back to reading for children and young people. It’s not an annual event. In fact, there have only been two other campaigns; in 1998 and 2008. In 2026, with smartphones and AI taking hold of our younger generations, the act of reading has taken a backseat. According to The National Literacy Trust, only 1 in 3 children and young people aged 3-18 currently enjoy reading in their free time, and only 1 in 5 read daily.

Research undertaken by the Department for Education has shown that children who are confident readers by the end of primary school can earn £65,000+ more over their lifetime compared to non-readers. The theme for the 2026 campaign is called ‘Go All In’, which encourages young people to read about their hobbies, interests and passions. This could include music, films, food and sport – using a wide range of different formats to make reading more culturally relevant, engaging and enjoyable.

items.title: What to Prepare Before Starting Your Fostering Journey
items.snippet: To help us understand what prospective foster carers should think about before making an enquiry, we spoke with Kate, one of our Foster Care Recruitment Coordinators. The post What to Prepare Before Starting Your Fostering Journey appeared first on Swiis Foster Care.
items.content:
Many people delay making a fostering enquiry because they think they need to have every detail organised first. In reality, the enquiry process is designed to help you explore whether fostering could be the right fit for you and your household.

While you do not need all the answers before contacting a fostering agency, there are some things worth considering in advance. Taking time to think about these areas can help the journey feel less overwhelming and give you a clearer understanding of what fostering might involve for you and your family.

To help us understand what prospective foster carers should think about before making an enquiry, we spoke with Kate, one of our Foster Care Recruitment Coordinators. Kate is often one of the first people applicants speak to when they begin exploring fostering. She guides prospective foster carers through those early conversations, answers questions and helps them understand what to expect throughout the assessment process.

Having supported hundreds of prospective foster carers over the years, Kate understands the concerns and misconceptions that can stop people from taking that first step. Drawing on her experience, we have explored some of the key things it can be helpful to think about before starting your fostering journey, from preparing your household and support network to understanding the assessment process and practical requirements of fostering.

If you are unsure whether fostering could be right for you, our Can I foster? quiz is a great place to start. It only takes a few minutes and can help you understand whether you meet the basic eligibility requirements.

Take Our Can I Foster? Quiz

Think About Your Spare Room

To foster, you will need a spare bedroom that can be used exclusively by a foster child or young person. Many prospective foster carers have a home office, guest room or storage room that they plan to use as their fostering bedroom.

The room does not usually need to be prepared at the enquiry stage. As you progress through the assessment process, your assessing social worker will discuss the room requirements with you and help you understand what is needed.

At this stage, it is more important to know the space is available than to have it fully furnished and ready to go.

Have Honest Conversations with Your Household

One of the most important things you can do before starting is talk openly with the people you live with.

Fostering is a household decision, not an individual one. During the assessment process, everyone living at home will have an opportunity to share their thoughts and feelings. Taking the time to discuss fostering now can help identify any questions or concerns early on.

You might want to have a chat about:

  • How fostering could affect your family routines.
  • How children and young people may become part of family life.
  • Whether household members are comfortable with the checks that form part of the assessment process.
  • What support everyone may need along the way.

Talk to the Children in Your Home

If you have children living at home, fostering will have an impact on them too. Having open and age-appropriate conversations can help them understand what fostering is and give them an opportunity to share how they feel about welcoming another child or young person into the family.

You could ask simple questions such as:

  • How would you feel about another child staying in our home?
  • Would you be happy to share some of your toys or space?
  • How would you feel about sharing Mum or Dad’s time with another child?

There is no right or wrong answer. The purpose is simply to start a conversation and ensure children feel included from the beginning.

Think About Your Support Network

While Swiis provides extensive support through supervising social workers, placement support workers, experienced fostering professionals and our 24-hour out-of-hours service, foster carers are also encouraged to have their own personal support network in place.

As part of the assessment process, you will be asked about the people around you who could offer practical or emotional support if needed.

Before enquiring, it can be helpful to think about:

  • Friends and family members you trust.
  • People who could help in an emergency.
  • Those you can talk to when you need advice or encouragement.

Many foster carers say having a strong support network is one of the things that helps them feel confident throughout their fostering journey.

Start Thinking About References

References are a standard part of fostering assessments and help us understand your life experiences, relationships and suitability to care for children.

References are not about looking for reasons to reject applicants. They help us build a picture of your relationships, experiences and support network so we can make informed decisions that keep children and young people safe.

While you do not need references at the enquiry stage, it can help to think about who you may ask later.

Typically, fostering assessments include:

Personal References

You will usually be asked to provide people who:

  • Have known you for several years.
  • Know you well.
  • Are not immediate family members.

Many applicants choose trusted friends, neighbours or colleagues.

Former Partner References

Understandably, this is something some people worry about.

A previous partner reference is not about judging past relationships or causing difficulties. It is a safeguarding requirement used across fostering services to help understand family history and ensure children’s wellbeing remains at the centre of decision making.

The assessment team understands that relationships end for many reasons and will discuss individual circumstances with you throughout the process. The key is openness and honesty rather than having a perfect past.

We also complete other background checks and references as part of the assessment. You can read more here:

Background Checks and References

Prepare Emotionally

One part of the fostering assessment that often surprises applicants is how reflective the process can be.

During the assessment, your assessing social worker will spend time getting to know you, your upbringing, family relationships, parenting experiences and significant life events. These conversations help build a fuller picture of who you are and the experiences that have shaped you.

For some people, this may mean discussing challenges, difficult periods in their lives or experiences they have not spoken about for some time. This is not about judgement. It is about understanding your resilience, support systems and ability to provide stability and care for children and young people.

The assessment is completed at your pace, and your assessing social worker will guide and support you throughout the process.

Be Ready to Learn

Many successful foster carers begin their journey without any professional childcare experience. The assessment and training process is designed to help you build your confidence, knowledge and skills along the way.

Training sessions, discussions with social workers and support from experienced professionals will help you develop the knowledge and skills needed to care for children and young people.

No one starts fostering knowing everything. What matters most is being open to learning, developing new skills and growing in confidence along the way.

Foster Care Training

Understand Why the Process Takes Time

The fostering assessment typically takes around four to six months. While this can feel like a long time when you are eager to start fostering, many parts of the process rely on external organisations returning information such as DBS checks, medical reports, local authority checks and references.

Although these checks can occasionally slow the process down, they play a vital role in safeguarding children and ensuring foster carers are fully prepared for the role.

The process may take time, but every stage exists for an important reason.

Find out more about each stage of the journey, from your initial application through to your first care arrangement:

Application to Arrangment Journey

A Little Preparation Can Go a Long Way

Before making an enquiry, take some time to think about how fostering could affect the people around you. Speak to your partner, children, family and friends. Consider who could support you during the assessment and who may be able to provide a reference later in the process.

You do not need to have everything planned before you begin. Having these conversations early can help you feel more confident and prepared when you take the next step.

Ready to Take Your Next Step?

If you are ready to explore fostering further, start by taking our Can I Foster? quiz, downloading our Fostering Info pack, or speaking with our friendly team for a chat.

You do not need to commit to anything straight away. We are here to answer your questions, explain the process and help you decide whether fostering is the right fit for you and your household.

items.title: Lynsey and Neil’s First Year with Swiis
items.snippet: After ten years as foster carers, Lynsey and Neil knew exactly what fostering could offer children and young people. The post Lynsey and Neil’s First Year with Swiis appeared first on Swiis Foster Care.
items.content:
After ten years as foster carers, Lynsey and Neil knew exactly what fostering could offer children and young people. They had supported children through significant milestones, cared for long-term placements, and built a wealth of experience along the way.

So, when they decided to move back to the North East from Lancashire with their four-year-old son, they knew they wanted to continue fostering. The challenge was finding the right agency to support the next stage of their journey. 

Now, almost a year after transferring to Swiis Foster Care, they are reflecting on their experience, the progress of the young person in their care and what has made their first year such a positive one.

Why did you decide to transfer to Swiis?

“When we moved back to the North East, I knew I wanted to continue fostering.”

“I did some research and looked at a few different agencies before coming across Swiis. Support is really important in fostering and that is one of the things that stood out to us with Swiis.”

Having spent a decade with another organisation, transferring felt like a big step.

“It was quite scary at first. You are building new relationships with new people, learning different policies and procedures and starting all over again with a different team.”

“But the experience has been a very positive one. From head office to our local Durham office, everyone has been really supportive and welcoming. We can only say it has been such a positive experience for us.”

How would you describe your first year with Swiis?

“There is a big network of people within Swiis. I have been fortunate that I have not needed to use out-of-hours support, but knowing it is there 365 days a year gives you peace of mind.”

“We have had amazing support from social workers, the health advisor, the training team and the office staff. If we have ever been unsure about something, there has always been someone there to help.”

One recent example came when they sought advice from Swiis’ Health Advisor about supporting their young person in their care.

“Katie, the Health Advisor gave us advice and tools we could use to help the young person manage things more independently. It was really helpful having someone with specialist knowledge to talk things through with.”

“We honestly cannot fault the support. If you need it, it is there in abundance.”

What have been the most rewarding moments?

One of the most rewarding aspects of Lynsey and Neil’s first year with Swiis has been supporting a young person with learning difficulties who came into their care almost a year ago.

When she first arrived, they quickly realised she needed support with many everyday skills.

“She was 13 but, of no fault of her own, and with her learning difficulties, there were lots of basic life skills missing. We had to go right back to the beginning and help her learn things like using cutlery, personal hygiene, brushing her hair and brushing her teeth.”

The progress she has made since then has been remarkable.

“The growth in twelve months has just been astounding. Things that are everyday tasks for most people were genuinely challenging for her, but now she is doing so much independently and with very little prompting.”

“She is much more settled at home, in her education, and she has made fantastic progress. When children are settled both at home and in school, you are halfway there to success.”

How has your journey been with Swiis’ training?

Although Lynsey and Neil had ten years of fostering experience, supporting a child with learning difficulties was new territory.

“This was our first time supporting a child with learning difficulties, so we have learned and grown together.”

“I honestly do not know if there is anything that Swiis does not cover through training. There are courses around ADHD, autism and so many other topics. The training helps you understand why children might react in certain ways and gives you practical tools to support them.”

“We have thoroughly enjoyed some of the training, and it has helped us understand our young person so much better.”

Becoming part of the Swiis Buddy Scheme

During their first year with Swiis, Lynsey and Neil were invited to become part of the Buddy Scheme, supporting newer foster carers as they begin their own journeys.

“I was really honoured to be asked. It was lovely knowing that somebody had seen qualities in us and felt we could support other foster carers.”

“The buddy scheme has been amazing. Sometimes it is easier to ask another foster carer a question because they are doing exactly the same job as you every day.”

“It has been really rewarding to support somebody through challenges, share experiences and help them feel more confident.”

How have you found the community in your new network of foster carers?

When talking about Swiis, one thing Lynsey returned to was the sense of community.

“When we go to the office, everyone knows who you are. It is very personal.”

“It feels more like being part of a family than working for an agency.”

She also spoke warmly about the events organised by Swiis throughout the year, particularly those focused on celebrating the achievements of children and young people.

“My favourite event was the achievement awards. Every child received recognition for something they had achieved, whether it was learning to swim, helping at home, tying their shoelaces, or getting great GCSE results.”

“Seeing those children so proud of themselves was incredibly emotional. It really showed how child-focused Swiis is.”

What are you looking forward to next in your fostering journey?

Recently, Lynsey and Neil received approval for their young person’s placement to become long-term.

For them, that means being able to continue supporting her through some of life’s biggest milestones.

“We are really looking forward to everything that is still to come. We would like to get her first passport, take her abroad for the first time and continue supporting her through school and into adulthood.”

“She could not tie a shoelace when she came to us, and now we are looking ahead to GCSEs and all the exciting opportunities in her future. Watching that growth is one of the most rewarding parts of fostering.”

What advice would you give to someone considering fostering?

“There is a huge support network around you, and it is there to help.”

“Fostering can be challenging at times, but it is also incredibly rewarding. We really need more foster carers because so many children need that safe place to call home.”

“I genuinely love what I do. Every day is different and watching children grow, develop and achieve things they never thought possible makes it all worthwhile.”

After ten years of fostering and a successful first year with Swiis, Lynsey and Neil are excited about the development of the children in their care. While every fostering journey is different, one thing is certain, their commitment to helping children reach their full potential remains as strong as ever.

If this story has inspired you to explore fostering, or if you would like to find out more about becoming a foster carer, contact our recruitment team. They will be happy to guide you through the fostering process, explain the support, training and allowances available, and answer any questions you may have.

items.title: A Summer Full of Fun in The North West
items.snippet: Our TACT North West team organised some fun and varied activities for our young people over the summer - with one young person completing an amazing personal challenge! The post A Summer Full of Fun in The North West appeared first on TACT.
items.content:
A Summer Full of Fun in The North West

TACT’s Fostering North West team were very busy over the summer holidays organising some brilliant activities for our young people. One of our young people even completed an amazing personal challenge!

We kicked off the summer with our Multi-Sports Activity Day, delivered by Sportibees. Following the success of this event last year, and after hearing so many positive comments from our children and foster carers, we were delighted to bring it back again. The day was packed with a variety of sports and activities, giving everyone the opportunity to get involved, try something new and have fun together!

Another one of our summer activities came directly from our young people, who asked if they could meet up for an escape room challenge. It was wonderful to see friendships that have developed over the years continue to grow and strengthen. Not only did everyone enjoy spending time together, but we’re pleased to report that all of our young people successfully escaped. A huge well done to them all!

Throughout the holidays, children and young people also enjoyed a range of other outings, including bowling trips, cinema visits, arcade afternoons and days out at local parks. These activities provided opportunities for fun, relaxation and they enjoyed spending quality time together.

We were also fortunate to join colleagues from TACT West Midlands and TACT East Midlands for the Children Who Foster Residential. This was a first for our two young people attending, making it an especially memorable occasion. They had the opportunity to meet and connect with other children who foster, building friendships and support networks that we hope will continue to grow long into the future. The residential was packed with exciting activities, including high ropes, bag jumps, zip lining and much more, creating experiences and memories that will last for years to come.

To round off the summer, we headed to Blackpool Pleasure Beach. Despite a few rainy spells, over sixty carers, young people and staff came together to enjoy a fantastic day of rides, laughter and fun. As well as being an opportunity for everyone to enjoy themselves, the day also provided a valuable chance for carers and children to meet new people, catch up with familiar faces and strengthen the sense of community that is so important across our service.

Alongside the group activities, we were also delighted to celebrate an individual achievement this summer. One of our young people took on the challenge of abseiling down Anfield Stadium. This was a remarkable accomplishment that required real bravery, and we are incredibly proud of them for embracing such an exciting opportunity.

We received some amazing feedback from our foster carers and young people:

  • “The boys always enjoy the activities and it was great to catch up with everyone!” – TACT Foster Carer
  • “When can we do another activity?” – TACT Young Person
  • “The older ones said they loved the big rides and were ‘made up’ to be big enough for the new ride! It was also perfect age-wise as there was something for all the kids so an all round perfect option for a day out” – TACT Foster Carer
  • “Thank you for the trip, we enjoyed it!” – TACT Young Person

A big thank you to our North West team for organising and facilitating these amazing activities for our young people!
