Making Memories at Llangrannog!
items.snippet: Our TACT Wales team organised and facilitated an exciting residential trip to Llangrannog for our young people! The post Making Memories at Llangrannog! appeared first on TACT.
items.content:
Making Memories at Llangrannog!

TACT’s Fostering Wales team took a group of young people on a residential trip to Llangrannog during the summer holidays – to try some new activities, spend some quality time together – and to create memories that will stay with them long into the future.

Eleven young people aged 8 to 13 attended from TACT, alongside nine children from our North Wales fostering partner, Foster Care Values (FCV). This was the first time FCV had taken their young people on a residential break, and it proved to be a very positive and successful experience.

From the very first evening, it was clear that friendships were beginning to form. The team-building activities helped everyone settle in, feel included and begin building trust with one another. Over the few days we were there, we could see confidence and independence growing in the young people. Some of the biggest highlights included walking down to the beach, splashing in the sea together (some fully dressed!) – and taking part in the tobogganing, which was fast, wet, exciting and full of laughter.

It was especially lovely to see so many of the young people try something new; they encouraged one another to step outside of their comfort zones by cheering each other on, and celebrating every achievement. Whether it was taking on a high jump onto a giant airbag or simply giving an unfamiliar activity a go, there were many proud moments and plenty of big smiles!

At the end of each busy day, it was just as meaningful to see everyone relax together; watching a film, eating popcorn, chatting about the day and sharing thoughts and life experiences in a calm and supportive space.

Feedback from our young people was wonderfully positive. Here are just a few of the comments we recieved:

  • “I have had fun with my friends and meeting new ones. I enjoyed getting splashed by the waves at the beach and feeling chilled there.”
  • “Llangrannog is the best place in Wales. I have already been here seven times with school and TACT. I love meeting friends.”
  • “You meet new friends for life. Go karting was my favourite activity.”
  • “I loved the experience. I had a great time, it was really fun and I made many friends that I’d love to see again.”

A big thank you to our Wales team for organising and facilitating such a wonderful trip for our young people!

Why Foster Carers Are Needed
items.snippet: Foster carers provide far more than a place to stay, they offer a safe and nurturing home where children can feel secure, rebuild trust and begin to thrive. The post Why Foster Carers Are Needed appeared first on Swiis Foster Care.
items.content:
Every child deserves to feel safe, valued and cared for. Yet across the UK, more than 81,000 children are currently in care, and over 7,200 additional fostering households are needed to meet growing demand.

Behind these statistics are children facing challenging circumstances who need stability, support and someone who will listen to them. Foster carers provide far more than a place to stay, they offer a safe and nurturing home where children can feel secure, rebuild trust and begin to thrive. Through kindness, encouragement and consistent care, foster carers help children develop confidence and look towards the future with hope.

As the demand for foster carers continues to grow, more people have the opportunity to make a lasting and meaningful difference in a child’s life, providing the support and security they need when it matters most.

The growing need for foster carers

More children are entering care each year, increasing the need for foster carers across the UK. When there are not enough local fostering households, children may have to move away from their siblings, schools, friends and support networks, creating even more disruption during an already difficult time.

Remaining close to familiar places and people can make a significant difference to a child’s emotional wellbeing. Local foster carers help children maintain routines, continue their education and stay connected to the communities that matter most to them.

Children come into care for many different reasons, through no fault of their own. While every child’s experience is unique, they all deserve a nurturing environment where they can begin to recover from difficult experiences and thrive.

Foster care is about more than providing a home

Fostering is about creating a stable and caring environment where every day routines such as sharing meals, getting ready for school, celebrating achievements and taking time to listen help children develop and build confidence.

With the right support, children are better able to engage with education, explore new interests and develop important life skills. Whether it is cheering from the sidelines at a football match, helping with homework or celebrating a school achievement, foster carers play an important role in encouraging children to reach their potential.

As young people grow older, foster carers also help prepare them for adulthood by teaching practical skills such as cooking, budgeting and planning for employment or further education. These experiences give young people greater independence as they move towards adult life.

The difference foster carers make

Often, it is the smallest moments that have the greatest impact. A calm conversation after a difficult day, a familiar morning routine, a packed lunch prepared with care or simply knowing that someone is there to listen can help a child feel safe and valued.

These everyday acts of kindness create the consistency many children have been missing. Over time, they help strengthen self-esteem and provide the foundation children need to achieve their potential.

As Swiis foster carer Bianca explains:

“We have witnessed growth in every way with both children, and their happiness knows no bounds. We are confident in our journey knowing that the children trust us.”

Read Bianca and Jermell’s Fostering Story

The voices of children and young people in our care offer an equally powerful reminder of the impact a loving foster family can have. In a personal letter about their experience in foster care, one young person wrote:

“[My foster carers] are the reason I am the person I am today… I feel like I will actually have someone to help me through any hard times I have, someone I can actually talk to about things. I am no longer afraid of growing up, because I know that I am surrounded by amazing people who will support me and be there for me through thick and thin.”

Have a read of the full ‘Why I want to stay with my foster carers’ letter

Why become a foster carer?

People choose to become foster carers for many reasons, but they all share a desire to make a meaningful difference to a child’s life.

Fostering can be both rewarding and challenging, requiring patience, resilience and understanding. While every fostering journey is different, Swiis foster carers are never expected to manage alone.

Many describe fostering as life changing, not only for the children they care for but for themselves as well. Watching a child overcome challenges and achieve milestones can be one of the most rewarding experiences a person can have.

How Swiis supports foster carers

At Swiis, we support foster carers throughout every stage of their fostering journey. From your first enquiry through to your care arrangement, you will be part of an experienced and supportive network.

Our foster carers receive comprehensive training, ongoing guidance and access to dedicated professionals such as health and education advisors, to help them provide the best possible care for the children they look after.

We are committed to helping children achieve positive outcomes while ensuring every foster carer feels respected and supported in their role.

Take the next step

By becoming a foster carer, you could provide the stability, encouragement and care that helps a young person build a brighter future. With more foster carers needed across the UK than ever before, your decision could make a lasting difference to a child’s life.

If you would like to find out more about becoming a foster carer with Swiis, our friendly recruitment team is here to help. They will be happy to guide you through the fostering process, explain the support, training and allowances available, and answer any questions you may have.

items.title: Putting Children Before Profit Starts with More Foster Carers
items.snippet: Residential homes for children are costing local authorities tens of thousands of pounds per week, and should be a wake-up call. But the issue runs deeper than money. The post Putting Children Before Profit Starts with More Foster Carers appeared first on TACT.
items.content:
Putting Children Before Profit Starts with More Foster Carers

A recent Times article highlighted the shocking reality that residential placements for children are costing local authorities tens of thousands of pounds per week. This should be a wake-up call for everyone involved in children’s social care. The costs are staggering – but the real issue goes deeper than money.  

Too many children are living in residential care because there simply aren’t enough foster families available to meet their needs. If we want to reduce the opportunity for profiteering in the care system, we need to increase the number of loving, well-supported foster homes children can move into. 

Of course, residential care has an important role to play in the sector. For some children, it is absolutely the right setting and can provide specialist support that cannot be delivered elsewhere. But for many children, a loving family home could offer the stability, relationships and sense of belonging they need to thrive. The challenge is that there simply aren’t enough foster carers willing and able to support them. 

That’s why TACT has launched Step Forward – a specialist fostering programme designed to help children move from residential care into stable family environments.

Step Forward Fostering provides enhanced support, therapeutic training, a strong network around carers and children, and a model specifically designed to support children who are currently living in a residential setting. 

For people with experience working with children, young people or in caring roles, Step Forward can also offer a meaningful alternative to a traditional career path. It provides the opportunity to use professional skills and life experience in a deeply personal, practical way, while receiving specialist training, wraparound support and a financial package that makes fostering a realistic option for people who may not previously have thought it was possible. 

As a not-for-profit fostering charity, we believe public money should be invested in children and families, not extracted as profit. Our focus is simple: better outcomes for children, stronger partnerships with local authorities, and greater social value for communities. If we want to reduce reliance on expensive residential placements, improve outcomes for children and create a more sustainable care system, we need more people to consider fostering. 

We need experienced, compassionate individuals who can help a child take the next step from residential care into family life. We need more people to Step Forward and help transform a child’s future.

Need for more ‘under 5’ foster carers in Scotland
items.snippet: There is an urgent need for more foster carers in Scotland to provide care for children under five years old. Why is this? The post Need for more ‘under 5’ foster carers in Scotland appeared first on TACT.
items.content:
Need for more ‘under 5’ foster carers in Scotland

Does the need for more foster carers to care for babies and ‘under 5’ children in Scotland point to a reduced pool of foster carers, more children coming into care – or are there more complex reasons?

It is an expected scenario that very young children are usually placed with a local authority’s own foster carers, with older children, or those with more complex needs, being referred to independent fostering agencies. However, since January 2026, 41% of TACT’s referrals from across Scotland have been for children aged under five. This has represented a significant shift in the age bracket of children being referred externally to fostering agencies.

There could be many reasons for this, and it is difficult to pinpoint any single factor. Let’s look at two most likely causes, what can be done – and what needs to change.

General decrease in foster carers in Scotland

Whilst it is difficult to access up-to-date statistics from other organisations, Plan 24-30 reported that between 2019 and 2024 the number of registered fostering households decreased by 21.8% in Scotland. Reasons for this are not easily identifiable, but could point to foster carers naturally retiring from the sector versus a decline in the number of new fostering households coming forward. In addition, budgets for carer recruitment marketing campaigns could be squeezed, reducing the active push for new carers.

The number of children and young people requiring care also fell during this period, but the number of available foster carers declined at a faster rate.

A reduced pool of foster carers across Scottish local authorities will, of course, result in those referrals for very young children being pushed out to external agencies.

But there lies our next problem.

External fostering agency carers not prepared for ‘under 5’s’

Many independent fostering agencies recruit their foster carers based on the traditional construct of providing care for older children, with those solely wishing to care for under fives being signposted to their local authority.

The reason why some foster carers may not be able to provide care for younger children could be that it does not fit their current household composition, skill set or preference. They would also need to be approved by a fostering panel to provide care for that age group.

Fostering infants and toddlers presents different challenges from fostering older children, as carers must provide highly responsive care that meets young children’s developmental, emotional, and health needs during the very important stage of early growth.

If external agency foster carers are not prepared to provide matched foster care for under fives, because they were never expected to, this could create an impasse if local authorities don’t have enough foster carers generally.

What can Fostering Providers do?

As a fostering charity, TACT will always aim to prioritise certain foster carer recruitment based on a demand for a specific type of fostering per region, alongside a more general recruitment push.

As previously mentioned, a focus on recruiting carers to provide care for under fives would usually be off the table for independent fostering agencies – but it is clear that this is not the case in Scotland. Local authorities would need to prioritise their own recruitment strategies, of course. Independent fostering agencies based in, or covering Scotland, should not only formulate integrated carer recruitment marketing campaigns aimed at providing care for the under fives – they should be looking to nurture and upskill their current foster carers, where possible.

As a charitable fostering agency, TACT’s focus has always been on the wider care system and great outcomes for children, over and above profit or traditional business focuses. By actioning specific carer recruitment and nurturing strategies, the sector would be providing a workable plan to help create a natural influx of foster carers able to provide care for the under fives in Scotland; a ‘call to arms’ outside of any one organisations’ own interests.

What needs to change?

Moving forward, there does need to be a general change in the way local authorities approach the referral and matching process for under fives and, in fact, all young people.

Referrals should call on both in-house local authority carers and external agency carers simultaneously – with the ‘best match’ being the goal in every single scenario. If more external agencies were to receive referrals for very young children, they would adapt their recruitment strategies to match demand. As it stands, there is a potential block when it comes to recruiting carers for under fives, because these referrals are traditionally pushed to local authority carers first.

This has been an historic issue for many years, and it does need to change. With a level playing field, children will not only benefit from the best match across their local authority and external agencies, it will also help create a wider pool of skilled foster carers able to care for children of all ages.

Sarah First Year Reflections
items.snippet: Over the past year, Sarah has welcomed children into her home and focused on building strong, trusting relationships, supported by her wider network and her dog, Gertie, who plays a special role in helping children feel safe and settled. The post Sarah First Year Reflections appeared first on Swiis Foster Care.
items.content:
Deciding to foster is a big step, and the first year in particular is a period of significant learning, growth, and connection. It brings a mix of new experiences, meaningful moments, and important milestones. It is the small, everyday interactions that often leave the biggest impact; building trust, creating routines, and forming bonds that matter. This first year is not just about change, but about laying the foundations for something truly meaningful, making fostering a journey well worth celebrating.

Sarah, one of our Midlands foster carers, has recently celebrated her first-year milestone in her fostering journey.

Over the past year, Sarah has welcomed children into her home and focused on building strong, trusting relationships, supported by her wider network and her dog, Gertie, who plays a special role in helping children feel safe and settled.

As she reflects on this first year, Sarah shares some of the moments that have shaped her journey as a foster carer with Swiis.

Looking back on your first year of fostering with Swiis, how would you describe the experience?

“Looking back on my first year of fostering, it has been a real learning journey. I have gained a much deeper understanding of how important clear boundaries are, and how they help create stability and safety for children in my care. Like many new foster carers, I learned a lot through experience, and those lessons have helped me grow in confidence and approach each care arrangement with greater clarity.”

“My first arrangement helped me understand just how resilient children and young people can be, even after experiencing significant challenges in their lives. Building trust took time, but when those moments of connection came, they felt incredibly meaningful.”

As a single foster carer, what has your experience been like, and what have you found most rewarding about fostering on your own?

“Fostering as a single carer has had its challenges, but it has also brought many positives. While there are moments when I need to pause and reflect on situations independently, I have learned how to process things calmly and confidently.”

“I am fortunate to have a supportive network around me, including my daughter and close friends, who I can talk things through with when needed.”

“Having that one-to-one time with the child in my care has helped us build strong bonds and develop trusting relationships.”

Can you share the types of support you received during your first year of fostering with Swiis, and how this support made a difference for you?

“The support I have received from my supervising social worker has been invaluable throughout my first year of fostering. Whenever I have had concerns or felt unsure about certain behaviours, she has been quick to respond, sharing helpful guidance and reassurance.”

“This guidance has supported my learning and helped me move forward with confidence and a more informed approach.”

“Jordon Murdoch, the stability and support manager has also been a lifesaver, offering practical advice and reassurance around managing different behaviours as they arise. I have also felt well supported by the out of hours service, which has given me real peace of mind.”

“All of this support has helped me feel part of a wider network that is there to guide, encourage, and support me to achieve the best possible outcomes for the child in my care.”

Your dog Gertie is such an important part of your home. How has she helped children feel more settled and comfortable?

“My dog Gertie has been remarkable with the children who come into my home. From the very beginning, they have felt safe and comfortable around her. She shows them so much love and affection which always helps bring out the best in them.”

“Animals can be a wonderful tool to help children learn empathy and gentleness and this has extended to other animals in the home too.”

“At one point I had ten chickens, which needed to be handled very carefully and this helped the children understand the importance of treating animals with compassion. When they show that care and kindness, they are rewarded with trust and show us lots of love in return, which was lovely to see.”

Can you share a particularly memorable experience from your first year of fostering with Swiis?

“There have been many positive moments that have stayed with me during my first year of fostering. When my first child began to open up and share her feelings, that was incredibly meaningful. Knowing that she trusted me enough to do so showed how far she had come and how safe she felt in my care.”

“My second child is full of energy. Every hug he gives me is memorable, as he means every squeeze, and those moments are a powerful reminder of the positive impact fostering can have.”

What advice or tips would you give to someone considering fostering as a single carer?

“I would highly recommend fostering to anyone who wants to make a genuine difference in a child’s life. I wish I would have done this years ago!”

“For single carers, having a good support network is really important, and with the right support behind you, fostering can be an incredibly positive and rewarding experience.”

Sarah’s first year with Swiis has been a journey of learning, growth and meaningful connection, she has felt supported and has asked for guidance when needed.  What a great first year, very well-done Sarah, we look forward to supporting you for many years to come.

If this story has inspired you to explore fostering, or if you would like to find out more about becoming a foster carer, contact our recruitment team. They will be happy to guide you through the fostering process, explain the support, training and allowances available, and answer any questions you may have.

items.title: A Wake-Up Call: Supporting Care-Experienced Young People into Work
items.snippet: NEET is a growing national challenge. TACT's Sian Biddlecombe and Sam Gray identify what is potentially driving the crisis, and what needs to be done. The post A Wake-Up Call: Supporting Care-Experienced Young People into Work appeared first on TACT.
items.content:
A Wake-Up Call: Supporting Care-Experienced Young People into Work

At the end of May 2026, the Department for Education published its Young People & Work Interim Report, shining a stark light on a growing national challenge: almost one million young people aged 16–24 in the UK are not in education, employment or training (NEET).

While the overall NEET rate for young people is 13.5%, this rises dramatically to 40% for care-experienced young people aged 19–21. This is not just concerning, it is a national crisis.

Behind these statistics are complex realities. Around 60% of young people who are NEET are economically inactive, meaning they are not currently seeking work. Even more striking, 60% have never had a job, despite 84% saying they want to work. This clearly shows that this is not about a lack of motivation – it is about barriers.

What is driving the NEET crisis?

The report highlights several key factors:

  • Health and wellbeing challenges: Rising levels of mental health needs and neurodevelopmental conditions are now a primary driver of young people becoming disconnected from work.
  • A changing labour market: Entry-level roles have declined, recruitment is increasingly automated, and apprenticeships have fallen by 40%.
  • Employer expectations: Many employers are seeking prior experience even for entry-level roles, alongside concerns about providing pastoral support.
  • Cuts to early intervention and prevention services: Reductions in funding across early years, SEND provision, youth services, and Further Education have reduced the support available to young people.
  • System barriers: 1 in 10 under-19s do not complete their course and 1 in 6 do not achieve a Level 3 qualification.
  • Practical barriers: lack of transport, housing costs, childcare, and even the upfront cost of uniforms or equipment can all prevent young people from taking their first steps into employment.

Why are care-experienced young people most affected?

For children and young people in care, these challenges are often intensified; disrupted education due to placement or school moves at critical stages, unmet support for children with Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND), and limited exposure to careers education and opportunities can all play a part.

If there are gaps in a young person’s Pathway Plan – a document that maps out a transition to independent living – this .can also make young people vulnerable, particularly if there is also delayed access to Personal Advisers.

There are also wider social impacts; loneliness among young people has surged since 2019, with 1 in 5 young adults having one or no close friends. Without strong social networks, access to opportunities becomes even harder. Lower aspirations due to a lack of visible role models is another potential factor.

As one quote from the report captures powerfully: “The opportunities might be there, but if no one in your immediate family or social circle does that sort of thing, you haven’t seen it – so you don’t believe you can be it.”

“The issue has an impact on confidence, independence, health, and future life chances.  Care-experienced young people have ambitions, talent, and potential. They want to work. Our role as professionals, carers, partners and communities is to ensure that the pathways are there, the support is in place, and the belief is built.  Every young person deserves the chance to see a future and to achieve it.”

Sian Biddlecombe, TACT’s Head of Education

How TACT’s Education Service is helping to tackle NEET

As a charity who has established their own Education and Health Services, along with a care-experienced community called Connect, TACT have already put in place a number of initiatives:

  • Early intervention and support from our qualified advisors: for our social workers, foster carers and young people when education placements are not meeting needs or when exclusions arise.
  • Investing in potential and growing passions: we use our aspirational funding and education funding to provide a range of experiences and opportunities – from music lessons and sports clubs to school trips abroad, right through to mentoring, tuition, books and tickets to theatre, sporting and cultural events.
  • Practical employability support: including revision skills, CV writing, applications and interview preparation with our Post-16 team.
  • Access to help and support with pathway planning: such as the Apprenticeship Academy course or UCAS application support.
  • TACT Connect, offering lifelong community and support: as well as continued access to our Post-16 advisors for help with employment and education issues.
  • Partnership working: with organisations such as Springpod, NNECL, Become and the Rees Foundation to expand access to work experience, mentoring and careers networks.
  • Access to mental health support and assessments via TACT’s Health Service.

NEET: What more needs to be done?

Whilst we are proud of the work we have already done here at TACT, there is always more to do. Early intervention is key, such as starting careers education earlier and then embedding careers conversations across all communications with young people. Identifying young people at risk of becoming NEET sooner would mean strategies could be put in place.

Employers would need to play their part too; employer engagement and access to work experience and real-world opportunities would help further down the line.

However, it is not simply about employment. The issue has an impact on confidence, independence, health, and future life chances.  Care-experienced young people have ambitions, talent, and potential. They want to work. Our role as professionals, carers, partners and communities is to ensure that the pathways are there, the support is in place, and the belief is built.  Every young person deserves the chance to see a future and to achieve it.

Sian Biddlecombe (Head of Education) and Sam Gray (Post-16 Advisor)

items.content:
This Is Not Just Fostering…this is Putting children’s outcomes first

Mechelle Holley, TACT’s Health Commissioning & Performance Manager

On why it is important that TACT’s dedicated Health Service provides timely mental health support to young people.

In an industry shaped by significant regulation, process, and procedure, it is important to look beyond compliance and ask the most important, and often most challenging, question: what does this child need to thrive, and how do we make that happen?

Why is the question difficult to answer?

This question is difficult not because we doubt its importance, but because social care systems are often shaped by thresholds, eligibility criteria, and available resources rather than individual need.

Children’s experiences of trauma, loss, and instability do not always fit neatly into service models, and professionals are often balancing competing pressures – from risk and cost to placement stability and capacity. Answering this question properly requires time, flexibility, and a willingness to work differently.

Despite these challenges, this mindset must underpin our approach within health commissioning, where we advocate for children and young people to access services that truly meet their psychological, mental health, and wellbeing needs.

For many children in care, their needs do not fit neatly into diagnostic categories or service criteria. Their distress is often expressed through behaviour, relationships, and emotional dysregulation – all of which require timely, relational, and trauma-informed responses. 

A timely response is key

When statutory pathways are unable to offer a timely response, commissioning becomes more than procurement – it becomes an ethical and moral responsibility. We recognise that local authorities face real financial pressures, particularly when funding services that should be provided through statutory provision. However, the impact of unmet need is felt most by children and those who care for them, through increased distress, instability, and strain on relationships.

Children should not bear the consequences of systems struggling to meet demand. Their needs must come first. Acting early not only prevents challenges from escalating but is also the most responsible and effective use of resources, ensuring children receive the right help at the right time.

Reinvesting to address gaps in provision

As a charity, TACT is committed to improving the life chances of children and young people. By reinvesting surplus back into services, we are able to support local authorities in addressing gaps in provision. This enables a shared approach, focused on practical solutions that ensure children receive timely and meaningful support. 

Our framework offer further strengthens this approach. It provides access to a wide and flexible range of services that can be tailored to each child’s individual needs. Rather than a one-size-fits-all model, we can connect children with support that works for them.

This flexibility allows us to respond quickly and effectively, helping children feel understood, supported, and able to thrive – this is putting children’s needs and outcomes at the heart of decision making.

items.title: Meet Rebecca Couch: Marketing Manager
items.snippet: As Marketing Manager at Swiis, Rebecca leads the team responsible for how fostering is explained, shared, and understood across Swiis’ website, social media, and wider content. The post Meet Rebecca Couch: Marketing Manager appeared first on Swiis Foster Care.
items.content:
For many people, the idea of fostering begins with a simple but important question: could they offer a child the support, stability, and safe home they need? It’s often a moment filled with hope and a desire to do something meaningful, balanced with understandable uncertainty about what fostering truly involves. Helping people feel informed, reassured, and supported at this early stage is where Rebecca and her team play a vital role.

As Marketing Manager at Swiis, Rebecca leads the team responsible for how fostering is explained, shared, and understood across Swiis’ website, social media, and wider content. From the first time someone visits the website to the stories that bring real experiences to life, Rebecca and her team ensure people receive the right information at the right time to make choices that feel right for them.

Rebecca has been with Swiis for three years, joining as a Marketing Executive before progressing into her current role. She now leads the marketing function, setting direction, supporting her team, and working closely with colleagues across the organisation to ensure Swiis’ values are reflected in everything we do. Her role combines insight, storytelling, and collaboration, transforming complex information into content that is clear, accessible, and inspiring.

Outside of work, Rebecca enjoys slowing down and spending time on creative pursuits. She loves baking and has recently developed a passion for gardening, finding real satisfaction in researching plants, caring for them, and watching them grow.

Rebecca also has a strong interest in film, having studied it at university, with her short films screened at festivals both across the UK and internationally. Her passion for storytelling continues to shape both who she is and the work she does at Swiis.

We sat down with Rebecca to talk about her journey into marketing within fostering, how she leads her team, and why thoughtful, values-led communication is so important in helping people explore fostering with confidence.

Your Role at Swiis

What is your job title and how long have you worked at Swiis?

“My title is Marketing Manager, and I have worked for Swiis for three years. The first year of that was spent working as the Marketing Executive, and the last two years I have been working as the Marketing Manager.”

Can you share your journey into becoming a Marketing Manager at Swiis?

“I started in marketing within a PR agency and then moved to an organisation that dealt with flight training for pilots. I then moved to Swiis to become the Marketing Executive.

A few months into my role, I started my CIM Diploma in Professional Digital Marketing. I wanted to do that because I did not study marketing at university and I wanted a greater understanding of the wider marketing ecosystem, including strategy and segmentation.

Swiis supported me with my diploma, and within a year of being the Marketing Executive I was promoted to Marketing Manager, which is where I am today.”

Could you tell us a bit about your role and what a typical day looks like?

“My role is very varied, and no two days are ever the same. Some days I will be working with external agencies or freelancers, booking photographers for events, or speaking to regional teams. Other days I will be more data focused, looking at website analytics and enquiries to see how content is performing.

A typical day starts by checking our social media and advertising accounts, reviewing my weekly to do list, and checking in with the marketing team.

I regularly review the team’s work, including blogs, graphics, and documents, and make sure everything is aligned, on brand, and consistent in tone of voice.

I also meet regularly with other teams, especially recruitment, to understand the trends they are seeing and how marketing can support them.”

Fostering Insights

How does your work help reach and support people considering fostering with the right information at the right time?

“Fostering is a huge, life changing commitment, and many people come to us with lots of questions about eligibility, finances, family impact, and support.

The role of the marketing team is to educate and inform prospective foster carers so they can gather all the information they need before making a decision.

We do this largely through our website, which includes information about fostering types, eligibility, finances, the assessment process, matching, and care arrangements.

We also have our free information pack, which we recently revised to reflect the real questions people ask us, and our monthly webinars for people who want to learn more but are perhaps not quite ready to take the next step yet.

Alongside this, our recruitment team is easily contactable through phone, email, WhatsApp, and live chat. Together, it is about giving people all the tools they need to feel informed about whether fostering is right for them.”

How do shared stories help people understand what fostering is really like?

“Case studies give a real voice and insight into the day to day lives of foster carers. People sometimes come to fostering with preconceived ideas, and these stories help show the realities while offering reassurance.

We gather stories from foster carers with a wide range of backgrounds, including LGBTQ+ carers, single carers, renters, and people who foster teenagers, so people can see themselves reflected in those stories.

One particularly powerful story we received was from a young person who wrote a speech explaining why they wanted to remain with their foster carers and read it in court. With permission, we shared it on our website and social media. It was a wonderful heartfelt speech, and it showed the true positive impact fostering can have on a young person’s life and future.

Have a read of the letter

That is what fostering is really about, the difference foster carers make.”

How do you collaborate with other teams to identify gaps in knowledge for prospective foster carers?

“I work closely with the recruitment team to understand the types of enquiries they receive, and the questions people are asking most frequently.

If there is a common knowledge gap, we look at ways to address it through blogs, website updates, social media content, or any other channel which would be beneficial to prospective foster carers.

We also work closely with local Swiis teams to support their marketing efforts and events to ensure everything remains consistent with our branding and tone of voice.”

When developing fostering campaigns, what message do you hope people take away?

“The one message I would love to get across is that fostering is a huge step, and it is completely normal to feel unsure or nervous.

The key message I would want people to take away is that with Swiis, you will not be alone on this journey. From the first enquiry, through assessment, once a child joins your home, and beyond, Swiis will be there every step of the way.

There is a vast amount of support available to our foster carers from the training team, social workers, foster buddy mentors, and the stability and support team, all working together to support our foster carers.”

Rebecca’s role highlights how important it is to feel informed, supported, and understood when considering fostering. By combining insight, creativity, and collaboration, Rebecca and her team help shape how fostering is experienced long before a child enters a home.

It goes beyond simply sharing information, focusing instead on building confidence, addressing uncertainty, and helping people take their first steps with confidence and reassurance, knowing they are supported from the very beginning.

If you are considering fostering and want to learn more, our team is here to support you with clear information, guidance, and reassurance at every stage. Get in touch to speak with our recruitment team or explore our fostering info pack.

items.content:
This Is Not Just Fostering…this is helping young people grow in confidence

Kelsie Carter, TACT Engagement & Activity Practitioner

On why the smaller moments can sometimes have the most impact.

When people think about fostering, they often focus on what happens within the foster home. What is sometimes less visible is the wider support around children and young people: the relationships, experiences and consistent care that help them feel safe, confident and valued.

As an Engagement & Activity Practitioner (EAP) at TACT, I support children both one-to-one and in group settings. This work looks different for every child, but every piece of it plays an important role in supporting them to thrive.

One-to-one support that makes a difference

One-to-one time allows space for children to feel seen and heard. This might be through an activity, a conversation, or simply being alongside them in a calm and consistent way.

For some young people, having dedicated time with someone who listens without judgement helps them build confidence, trust and self-belief. At other times, this support helps children through tricky moments, supporting them to manage big emotions or talk through challenges. Often, it’s the small, quiet moments that create the biggest impact.

Building confidence through activities

Activity days are a key part of my role and offer children something equally important – a sense of belonging.

Group activities allow young people to connect with others who may have similar experiences, helping them feel less alone. Through shared activities, they can have fun, develop social skills and build friendships in a supportive environment.

Recent activity days have included Forest School Fun, an interactive animal day, our Annual Awards Ceremony at Weston-super-Mare Pier, and an upcoming group trip to Legoland which everyone is very much looking forward to!

Small moments that have a lasting impact

The work EAPs do is made up of many small moments — a conversation, a shared activity, a quiet word of encouragement. On their own, these moments might seem simple, but together they mean so much more.

By giving children our time, consistency and care, we help them build confidence, resilience and a belief in themselves.

items.content:
This Is Not Just Fostering…this is about social responsibility

Ramona Catarig, TACT’s Operational Director of Children’s Services

On why it’s important to be focused on the the long‑term social impact of the choices we make every day.

When people in the sector talk about fostering, the focus is often on placements – availability, cost, speed. But if that is where the conversation starts and ends, I believe we miss what really matters.

At TACT, we are deliberate about not using the word placement. For us, fostering has never been just about providing a home. It is about the responsibility we hold to children, to foster carers, and to the wider care system. It is about the long‑term social impact of the choices we make every day.

A responsibility rooted in purpose and values

Every child who comes into care carries a story shaped by instability, loss or trauma. Our first responsibility is, of course, to that child – to ensure they are safe, supported and able to thrive. But our responsibility does not stop there.

We also hold responsibility to:

  • Foster carers who step forward with commitment and compassion
  • Local authorities working under immense pressure
  • Care systems that are stretched, complex and in need of sustainable solutions
  • Public money that must be used wisely, transparently and ethically

Fostering, done well, creates stability for children/young people. Stability changes outcomes. And better outcomes reduce pressure on the whole system.

This is where fostering moves beyond service delivery and becomes a matter of social responsibility.

Why partnerships matter more than ever

Children’s services do not exist in silos, and neither do the challenges facing the sector.

Rising complexity, tighter budgets and growing demand mean that no single organisation can succeed alone. Social responsibility today means stepping into partnership: sharing insight, building trust and planning for the long term.

At TACT, this means working alongside commissioners, social workers and system leaders to:

  • Understand sufficiency pressures, not just react to them
  • Use shared intelligence to plan responsibly
  • Design services around outcomes, not transactions
  • Contribute to sustainable care systems, not short‑term solutions

This approach is not defined by volume or visibility, but by care, openness and values‑led decision‑making.

A charity with a system role

As a charity, we carry a particular responsibility. We are accountable not to shareholders, but to children and to the public good.

That responsibility is evident every day, through our commitment to evidence‑informed practice and our willingness to ask difficult questions about whether our work genuinely supports positive outcomes for children/young people – and strengthens the system. Crucially, it requires us to consider the long‑term impact of our decisions on children, carers and communities.

Fostering is changing. Commissioning is changing. Expectations are changing too. The organisations that will make a real difference are those that recognise fostering is not simply a service to be delivered, but a social commitment to stability, responsibility and partnership.

At TACT, we are proud to stand for that commitment. When we get this right, the impact is far reaching. This is not just fostering. It is shaping lives. It is strengthening communities. It is helping to build a care system that truly works for children/young people.

items.title: This Is Not Just Fostering…this is relational repair
items.snippet: TACT Step Forward hub foster carer, Caroline, talks about the key approaches for when young people transition from residential care to a fostering home. The post This Is Not Just Fostering…this is relational repair appeared first on TACT.
items.content:
This Is Not Just Fostering…this is relational repair

Caroline, TACT Foster Carer Since 2025

On key approaches for young people moving from residential care to a fostering environment.

TACT step forward hub foster carer, Caroline, is a registered Creative Arts Psychotherapist. She talks about the importance of using a trauma-informed approach when young people transition from residential care, and why it is an evolutionary process.

A hub carer is retained full time to support up to six young people along with their step forward foster carers. They offer advice and support, and work closely as a part of the wider support team.

This is relational repair. Not the kind of repair that is neat or linear. Instead, the kind that happens slowly, often quietly, through experience rather than explanation.

Many of the children who come into fostering, particularly those who have lived in residential care or experienced early adversity, are carrying developmental trauma. Their nervous systems, their expectations of adults, their sense of self have all been shaped by environments where safety, consistency, and attunement have not been reliably present.

So what we often see makes sense. The pushing away of care, the need for control, the quick move to fight, flight, freeze, or shut down and the testing of relationships – again and again.

These are not behaviours to fix. They are children’s adaptations to survive. Fostering, when it is trauma-informed, offers something fundamentally different.

It is the repeated experience of:

  • Someone staying when things feel hard
  • Someone responding with curiosity rather than consequence
  • Someone holding boundaries without withdrawing connection

Protective relationships – consistent, attuned, emotionally available, are one of the most powerful ways we can mitigate that impact.

In the Step Forward programme, that difference is often felt in the shift from residential care, where relationships can be caring but necessarily shared across staff – to a family home, where relational care is built and lived day-by-day, steady enough for trust to begin taking root.

Fostering can offer a different experience of adults, a different experience of safety and a different story about self and worth.

Over time, this begins to shift something deeper. Not because a child is told they are safe – but because they start to feel it.

This is not just fostering…it’s making space to welcome another child

items.content:
This Is Not Just Fostering…it’s supporting our people

Daniella Jackson, TACT’s Director of People

On why a stable, values-driven workforce can better provide high quality care.

Our Foster Care Fortnight campaign this year shines a spotlight on TACT and how we set ourselves apart from other organisations in the sector – This is not just fostering. This is TACT Fostering.

From a people perspective, this statement rings true every day. We have over 200 colleagues who support, enable and stand alongside our foster carers and young people, and who make the TACT culture what it is today.

We know that fostering is demanding, emotional and complex work. Supporting it well takes more than systems and processes; it takes purpose and a commitment to people, which is where TACT’s difference shines through.

Creating a workplace built around purpose and values

As an organisation, we’re led by our core purpose, values and trauma-informed principles. For our colleagues, this means knowing that their work genuinely makes a difference and contributes to better outcomes for children and young people.

We recruit and develop people based on our values to help create teams where trust, empathy and mutual respect are the norm. This also underpins our culture of belonging, where everyone is encouraged to bring their whole selves to work and feels safe to have open and honest conversations.

Supporting people who support others

Knowing the challenging nature of our work, we take a proactive approach to wellbeing, support, listening and recognition.

From manageable caseloads and regular supervision to flexible working and access to wellbeing sessions and resources, we’ve created an environment where our colleagues can do their best work without burning out. We also know how important it is to recognise a job well done, which is why we have an active Pass the Praise scheme and regular opportunities to say ‘thank you’ or celebrate sparkle moments.

Colleague voice is also something we take seriously, and feedback shapes our policies, benefits and the way in which we work. Our colleague’s voice’s matters and helps us to make improvements year-on-year.

Growing and developing at TACT

At the heart of our mission is a commitment to delivering great outcomes for children and young people. We believe that outstanding foster care begins with outstanding people and that means investing in their growth.

For our colleagues, this includes:

  • Ongoing learning and development tailored to real life challenges
  • Leadership development pathways and support
  • Opportunities for progression that do not require leaving frontline roles

Over the last year, we’ve been aligning our foster carer learning and development with our colleague programme. We now have a trauma-informed and child-centred approach to equipping foster carers with the knowledge, skills, and confidence to meet the complex needs of the children they care for, and this is something we’ll be developing year-on-year.

Why this all matters

All of these things we have in place (and much more!) have a direct impact on the children and young people we support. A stable, values-driven workforce is better able to provide consistent and high-quality care.

We know that when we invest in our people properly, we create a system that works better for everyone involved. And that’s what makes us different.

items.title: Pam’s fostering journey: 25 years of making a difference
items.snippet: For Pam, fostering has never been just a role. It is something she has felt drawn to from an early age, shaped by her own experiences and carried through into a lifelong commitment to children and young people. The post Pam’s fostering journey: 25 years of making a difference appeared first on Swiis Foster Care.
items.content:
“Fostering gives me a purpose and allows me to feel that I am doing something worthwhile and that I am making a difference.”

For Pam, fostering has never been just a role. It is something she has felt drawn to from an early age, shaped by her own experiences and carried through into a lifelong commitment to children and young people.

Since becoming a foster carer in 2001 with Swiis Midlands & South, Pam has supported many children, built meaningful relationships, and created a stable and caring home environment for every child in her care. We spoke with Pam to better understand the lasting impact that fostering can have not only on children, but also on the foster carers themselves.

Pam’s introduction to fostering came early in life. With both her parents working in children’s homes, she experienced first-hand the importance of providing safe and nurturing environments for children in care.

“I had known for a long time that I wanted to foster. My parents had worked in children’s homes. They took me to visit one when I was a child and the way it was set up into individual homes with live-in house parents impressed me.”

“When I became a foster carer, my parents were enthusiastic to share fostering knowledge that I did not yet have, often drawing on their own life experiences. They truly enjoyed being part of my fostering journey, supporting me every step of the way until they sadly passed away.”

Before beginning her fostering journey, Pam chose to wait until her daughter was older, while continuing her commitment to working with and supporting children.

“I worked in a nursery while my daughter was young and later continued working with children when I returned to education. I never lost my interest in fostering and was eventually approved to foster in 2001.”

Over the years, Pam has developed her own approach to fostering, shaped by experience and the relationships she has built.

“Every child is different, and each brings their own experiences. Your experience as a foster carer is unique to you and shaped by your home dynamics, which continue to evolve over time through the relationships you build.”

“I have had many different connections with the children and young people I have cared for, and each is special in its own way. Different things remind me of them, many of whom are not so young anymore.”

This adaptability has been key to her long-term success as a foster carer, and having consistent support from Swiis has been an important part of that journey.

“Swiis have been the one constant in my fostering journey. I have had invaluable support, from helpful suggestions to simply having someone to talk things through with, to the training I am truly grateful for. All of the children I have cared for have been so memorable and stand as a powerful reminder of the difference fostering can make, even short-term arrangements can have a lasting impact.

One of the things that had a big impact on me was when I was contacted by a boy that I had only cared for during a couple of short periods. He contacted me to say he’d welcomed his first baby and to thank me for being there for him. This really highlighted to me that although he only stayed in my care for a short time, it had still made a real impact on his life. Fostering gives me a purpose and allows me to feel that I am doing something worthwhile and that I am making a difference.”

Supporting children has been a consistent part of family life throughout Pam’s fostering journey. Her daughter has continued that connection, working in similar roles, sharing ideas and experiences.

“My daughter has always worked with children, often in roles that relate to mine, so we both share any useful information about places to go and things to try. She has been on some of our holidays and loads of trips out with us, as have her children, who usually become friends with the young people in my care.”

After more than two decades, Pam’s commitment to fostering remains as strong as ever. She also offers honest and reassuring advice to those considering fostering.

“I would feel lost without fostering. My whole life revolves around what I do, it is the main part of who I am. As with everything else in life, it will have its ups and downs, but it is useful to take a step back and look at the bigger picture and you will see how far you have come and how much progress there has been.”

Pam’s 25 year fostering journey shows that fostering is not just about individual moments, but about long-term impact, consistency, and care.

Through every arrangement, every relationship, and every moment of support, she has made a meaningful difference. Her journey reflects what fostering is truly about: providing stability, building trust, and helping children and young people move forward with confidence.

Inspired by Pam’s story?

Start your fostering journey today with the support of our experienced team. We will guide you every step of the way with training, advice, and reassurance. To learn more, get in touch with our recruitment team, who can answer any questions you have, or hear from other foster carers by reading more of our stories.

items.content:
This Is Not Just Fostering…it is a promise to a child’s future

Jessica Jackson, Area Manager For TACT East Midlands

On why it’s important to be future-focused when making fostering decisions.

Fostering is often described in practical terms; providing a home, meeting needs, offering care but that framing only scratches the surface of what it really entails. At its heart, fostering is a promise, a commitment that says: your story matters, your experiences will be understood, and your future is worth investing in.

A trauma-informed approach is essential

For many children, the journey into care comes with loss, uncertainty, and trauma. What they need is not just a safe place to stay, but a space where they can begin to feel safe within themselves. That doesn’t happen by accident. It takes consistency, patience, and a deep understanding of how trauma shapes behaviour, relationships, and identity.

This is why a trauma-informed approach isn’t an optional extra or an add on, it’s essential. When we understand that behaviour is communication, we respond differently. We look beyond what we see on the surface whether that’s anger, withdrawal, or dysregulation and without judgement we ask, ‘what has this child experienced, and what do they need right now?’. Creating safety, stability, and belonging with unconditional positive regard means holding that child in mind, especially in the moments when it feels most challenging.

Working within a not-for-profit organisation like TACT brings that promise into sharper focus. When profit is not the driver, decisions can be guided by what truly matters: the wellbeing and long-term outcomes for children. Resources are reinvested into support for foster carers, therapeutic services, training, and community which builds a system around the child that is thoughtful, responsive, and continually learning.

That commitment to learning is key. Trauma-informed care is not a fixed model; it evolves as we deepen our understanding of children’s needs, as research grows and evidence is developed. Being part of an organisation that invests in reflection, development, and evidence-informed practice means we are always asking how we can do better and then taking steps to make that happen.

Fostering, then, becomes more than a role. It becomes a shared responsibility, held not just by carers but by the wider organisation. It is about creating environments where children are not only safe but seen; not only cared for, but understood.

Because when we say fostering is a promise to a child’s future, we mean that every interaction, every decision, and every investment is shaping what comes next. And that is something worth getting right.

Meet Claire Hobson: Yorkshire Registered Manager
items.snippet: As Registered Manager, Claire Hobson sits at the very heart of the Yorkshire service, providing outstanding leadership and direction for the team. The post Meet Claire Hobson: Yorkshire Registered Manager appeared first on Swiis Foster Care.
items.content:
At the heart of every foster care service is a team of people deeply committed to doing the very best for children and young people. From foster carers to support staff and administrators, every individual plays a vital role in helping achieve positive outcomes for children and young people.

As Registered Manager, Claire Hobson sits at the very heart of the Yorkshire service, providing outstanding leadership and direction for the team. Claire has been part of the Swiis team for over a decade and has played a key role in shaping the Yorkshire service into what it is today. Claire leads a team that cares deeply, supports one another, and keeps children at the heart of everything they do.

Outside of work, Claire enjoys keeping life simple and spending time outdoors. She loves exploring the UK in her little campervan with her two miniature Schnauzers, who are at the centre of everything she does. She really values time with her adult children and is excited to become a grandma soon! When she is at home, you will often find her in the garden, growing her own vegetables and flowers.

We sat down with Claire to learn more about her journey, her approach to leadership, and what makes Swiis feel like a community built on shared values, care and purpose.

Your Role at Swiis

What is your job title, and how long have you worked for Swiis?

“I’m very proud to be the Registered Manager of the Yorkshire Service at Swiis. I started in the role in 2015, and in the ten years I’ve been here, the service has changed beyond recognition. When I first joined, we were a very small service with big ambitions, and it has been incredible to watch us grow not only in size, but in confidence, expertise and capability. We have built a service grounded in strong values, reflective practice and genuine teamwork.”

“Despite how far we have come, we have never lost the desire to keep learning. That is something I truly love about working at Swiis: we never stand still. We constantly look at how we can do better, be better, and offer more.”

Can you share your experience working in fostering and your journey into becoming a Registered Manager?

“I began my social work career a little later than most people. I decided to do my social work degree when I had 3 small children at home to look after! I worked for a Local Authority in a few frontline roles before finding fostering. I started as a supervising social worker, progressing to a fostering service manager role for a very large service of 300 fostering households. I then spotted the role of Registered Manager for Swiis, I researched the company and liked what I read, and the rest is history as they say.”

Could you share a bit about your role, what it involves and what a typical day tends to look like for you?

“The Registered Manager role is such a huge role, as registered managers are responsible for all that happens under our leadership. I spend a significant amount of my time analysing what is working well and what may need tweaking or changing completely to make the service more effective. I work with other Swiis Registered Managers across the regions who are a talented bunch, and we have support from very experienced senior colleagues. No two days are the same, and nothing surprises me anymore.”

“I work hard to ensure that our team share a clear understanding of why we do what we do. By continually linking our practice back to Swiis’ values of safety, respect, high-quality care, and integrity, we stay aligned and consistent. I aim to be encouraging and approachable so that the team feel confident to bring ideas forward, take ownership, and grow in their roles.”

In the recent Yorkshire Outstanding Ofsted result, Ofsted noted that the leadership team shared a clear vision and worked cohesively to promote excellent outcomes for children. How do you lead your team to bring Swiis’s values to the work you do?

“I don’t see myself as a standout leader on my own, I see myself as part of a team that is committed to the same purpose. My role is to guide, support, and create the right conditions for people to do their best work. I approach leadership calmly, always with the children at the centre of every decision we make. I bring Swiis’ values into daily practice by encouraging open communication, reflective discussions, and a culture where challenges are met with solutions rather than stress. I truly believe that there is never a problem too big to be resolved when we face it together, and I make sure the team feel supported and reassured, especially in pressured moments.”

“For me, leadership is about collaboration and modelling calm, steady decision‑making. We succeed because we support one another, challenge each other professionally, and stay united in our commitment to every child. When the team feel valued, trusted, and supported, the children experience the stability and quality of care they deserve, and that’s what truly reflects Swiis’ values in action.”

Read the Yorkshire Ofsted Report

Fostering Insights

Ofsted also noted that ‘The agency works effectively with a range of health, education and social care professionals.’ – What types of support is available to Swiis foster carers and how does it help them in their role?

“Foster carers do an extraordinary job, and at Swiis, they are never expected to do it alone. The support available is wide‑ranging because every child and every foster carer deserves to feel fully supported by the network around them. Foster carers have their own dedicated supervising social worker who works with a small number of foster carers and are available to foster carers to ensure the fostering arrangements’ success.”

“Our foster carers benefit from the expertise of a Health Advisor monitoring children’s health needs, providing specialist advice on areas of health and working directly with foster carers while coordinating with wider health services. They ensure foster carers never feel out of their depth when supporting a child with more complex health needs.”

“Our education specialist is also part of the support network, working with foster carers and schools to understand each child’s learning needs, help resolve educational challenges, or support with sourcing a suitable school. Their involvement contributes to the strong educational outcomes Swiis’ children and young people achieve and helps foster carers stay informed and confident in advocating for the young person’s learning journey.”

“Our placement support workers offer practical hands‑on help to foster families, facilitating a wide range of child-led activities and spending one‑to‑one time with the children and young people, focusing on aspects of their lives they may find more difficult to navigate. Their flexible support reduces pressure on foster carers and strengthens the stability of the arrangement. They are an innovative team who are always seeking our young people’s views and exploring their talents.”

Are there particular moments with foster carers or children and young people that have made you feel especially proud?

“In the ten years I have been with Swiis, there have been countless moments where I have felt incredibly proud of our children and young people. I am genuinely in awe of them on a daily basis. Hearing about their lives, the new things they are trying, the achievements they are proud of, and how their fostering families have helped make their futures feel a little less daunting, those moments stay with me.”

“Some of the most meaningful experiences for me are when I look back at foster carers I met right at the start of my journey, many of them are still fostering today. I have watched children I once helped to move in, grow up, turn 18, and still feel connected to their fostering family, and in many ways part of our Swiis family too. That brings me a real sense of pride, a shared pride that belongs to everyone who has supported that child along the way. Those moments remind me why we do what we do. They ground me, they inspire me, and they make me incredibly grateful to be part of a team that helps shape such positive futures.”

What is one piece of advice you would give to someone considering becoming a foster carer?

“I would say: don’t worry. If you have a big heart, patience, understanding, and a genuine desire to give a child the best possible start, then a foster carer might be exactly what you are meant to be.”

“Children have incredible potential, and they deserve a warm, loving home where they can feel safe, valued and believed in. You do not need to have all the answers on day one. What matters is that you truly care and that you are willing to learn. At Swiis, you are never on your own. If you are open to receiving help from experienced, skilled people who will walk the journey with you, then you will always have the support you need to tackle whatever comes your way.”

“So, if your heart is telling you that you want to make a difference, then honestly, what are you waiting for? It could be the most rewarding decision you ever make, for you and for a child who just needs someone in their corner always.”

Claire’s experience, compassion, and leadership remind us why fostering matters. It’s not about having all the answers, it’s about showing up, being supported, and making a difference together.

If Claire’s words have inspired you to explore fostering, why not do the Can I Foster Quiz, or contact our lovely recruitment team, who will be happy to walk you through the fostering process. Alternatively, have a read of our Fostering Info Pack for information on fostering and fostering with Swiis.

The Next Generation of Foster Carers – Mobeen’s Fostering Story
items.snippet: Becoming a foster carer at a younger age has allowed Mobeen to bring energy and a fresh perspective to the role, while still offering the structure, commitment and support that fostering requires. The post The Next Generation of Foster Carers – Mobeen’s Fostering Story appeared first on Swiis Foster Care.
items.content:
At just 27 years old, Mobeen stepped into a life-changing role when he was approved as a foster carer for Swiis. Since 2020, Mobeen, alongside his wife, Zara, have opened their hearts and home to children and young people from across the region. Their extraordinary commitment showcases a vibrant new generation of foster carers ready to take up the mantle.

By choosing to foster in their 20s, they are proving that you do not have to wait until later in life to make a lasting impact. Becoming foster carers at a younger age has allowed them to bring energy and a fresh perspective to the role, while still offering the structure, commitment and support that fostering requires.

We spoke with Mobeen about what inspired him and Zara to foster, what it is like being younger foster carers, and what they have learned since beginning their journey with Swiis.

Looking back, before you became a foster carer, was there a particular moment, experience, or influence that encouraged your decision to pursue fostering?

“Since my wife and I got married, we were always thinking about doing something for the community, and we spoke about fostering. But it was always in the background because we were working, or something always came up.

When our first daughter was born, that was the nail on the head for us. Looking at her made us think about what we could do as parents to help and provide for a child who is in a bad situation. That was the initial big step for us.

From there, we started to look into fostering agencies, reading case studies, and watching YouTube videos. My wife came across Swiis as one of the main organisations. From then on, we started looking more into what Swiis provides, and we took the first step by reaching out to get more information.”

How did your friends and family react when you first shared your plans to foster?

“They were incredibly supportive, which we didn’t quite expect. We are Asian Pakistani, and there are not many Asian Pakistanis who foster, so it is not something that’s common in our community. It was unfamiliar, but everyone was supportive. Some even started to question why they hadn’t thought about doing it before.

Sometimes you don’t realise the need for fostering because there isn’t a lot of information about it, or you don’t really notice it. You might walk past a billboard and not think twice. But there are so many children out there who need a foster home, and not enough people are applying to become foster carers. So, once they started to understand the need, they fully supported our decision.”

Choosing the right agency is a big decision in fostering, in your words, what made Swiis feel like the right agency for you as a younger foster carer?

“When my wife was on maternity leave after our first daughter was born and I was at work, she researched all the fostering agencies in our area. When I came home from work, I would look into them more deeply as well.

Agencies can seem very similar, so we asked ourselves what kind of support they could give us. We were going to be first-time carers, and it can be scary going into it. We wanted reassurance about what would be in place if something didn’t go quite right.

I researched anything I could find and asked a lot of questions, and Swiis ticked a lot of boxes for us. There was training provided, a strong matching process so the child and family are more likely to be the right fit, and an out-of-hours service for issues late at night. There is always a network of support and a social worker to handle queries, and if your social worker isn’t available, there is always someone else there.

That kind of support gives reassurance. If something does go wrong, you know what to do and who to contact.

Swiis also offers training throughout the year. When COVID hit, it moved online. That actually worked well for me because I work from home, so it was easier for me to attend instructor-led training online.

Overall, it was the backing and knowing that Swiis would be there, and that you would not be left on your own once you started fostering. That reassurance was what we needed, especially as first-time carers.”

What helps you to connect with the children or young people you care for?

“What helps me connect with the children and young people I care for is getting involved in their day-to-day lives and having fun together. Having played Xbox and PlayStation myself, I can join in with them, play games together, and enjoy their hobbies alongside them.

Sharing these experiences makes it easier to chat, laugh, and just spend quality time together. Taking an interest in what they love helps build trust and strong connections, which makes a real difference in how supported and understood they feel.”

Can you share a special memory or moment that made you feel especially proud of your decision to foster?

“We have quite a few, but one of the main ones was our first young person. They are transgender, and it took them a while to get placed with the right match. For us, we were open to any type of child. A child does not choose to be in that situation, and they should be given equal opportunity regardless of what they believe or who they want to be.

Someone being transgender was completely new to us, and there were challenges, but we were willing to learn. Over time, we saw a big change in the young person. When they first came, they were not confident and were very reserved. By the time they turned 18 and moved on to start a new life, they were much more confident and settled and seeing that change was a proud moment for us.

Another proud moment is with a young Muslim girl who has been with us for five to six years now. She has SEN needs and has issues with trust at the beginning due to neglect, but over time, she slowly opened up to us.

She went from struggling to string a sentence together to now being in her third year of college. She is able to catch buses on her own and attend appointments like the dentist or doctor. She has grown into a young adult who can do so much more for herself.

Seeing that transition and knowing we played a part in that makes us proud. It reassures us that we are doing the right thing.”

If there is someone out there in their 20s thinking about fostering but feeling a bit nervous, what would your advice be? What is the one thing you wish someone had told you before you took the leap at 27?

“Take the leap, just do it!

If you are worried about certain scenarios, Swiis is there for you. They have out-of-hours numbers and support systems in place for unexpected situations.

If you feel you do not have enough experience, they provide all the training.

There is a whole network within Swiis that you can reach out to. You can speak to foster carers, someone in training, or a social worker who has dealt with different situations.

You are not alone in it, and that is the most important thing.”

Mobeen and Zara’s fostering journey with Swiis shows that age is no barrier to making a meaningful difference. As younger foster carers, they have brought energy, commitment, and compassion to the role, helping to create stability and opportunity for the children and young people in their care.

Their story highlights how fostering can have a truly positive and lasting impact, not only shaping a child’s future but also enriching your own life as well.

If Mobeen and Zara’s journey has inspired you to explore fostering, or if you would like to find out more about becoming a foster carer, contact our recruitment team. They will be happy to guide you through the fostering process, explain the support, training and allowances available, and answer any questions you may have.
